The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $k\subseteq K$ be a field extension, and let $S\subseteq K$ be
algebraically independent over $k$. Assume that $S$ is maximal for inclusion
among algebraically independent subsets of $K$. Then every element of $K$ is
algebraic over the generated subfield $k(S)$, so $S$ is a transcendence basis
of $K$ over $k$.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.
If $F\subseteq K\subseteq L$, the extension $K/F$ is algebraic, and $L/K$ is algebraic, then $L/F$ is algebraic.

derivations.claim: Let $F\subset\Omega$ be a field extension with $\Omega$ algebraic over $F$, let $F_0$ be an intermediate field, and let $\phi_0:F_0\to\Omega'$ be an embedding into an algebraically closed field $\Omega'$. Order all extensions $\phi:E\to\Omega'$ with $F_0\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$ by extension. A chain has the union embedding, so Zorn's lemma from [F3] gives a maximal one. If $E\ne\Omega$, choose $\alpha\in\Omega\setminus E$; it is algebraic over $E$. Apply $\phi$ to its minimal polynomial and choose a root $\beta\in\Omega'$. The transported minimal polynomial is irreducible over $\phi(E)$ because $\phi$ is an isomorphism onto its image, so sending $\alpha$ to $\beta$ extends $\phi$ to an embedding of $E(\alpha)$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\phi$ extends to $\Omega$. If $\phi_0$ maps $F$ onto $F$ and both source and target are algebraic closures of $F$, this extension is onto: its image is algebraically closed and contains $F$, so it contains every root of every polynomial over $F$, hence all of $\Omega$.

Use [F2] to view $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ as a subfield of $\mathbb C$. By [F1], choose a transcendence basis $B$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$. Then $\mathbb C$ is algebraic over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ and, being algebraically closed, is an algebraic closure of that field.

If $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ but $z\notin\mathbb Q$, its irreducible minimal polynomial has degree at least two and has distinct roots because its derivative is nonzero and relatively prime to it. Choose another root $z'\in\overline{\mathbb Q}$. By step 1.1, the embedding $\mathbb Q(z)\to\overline{\mathbb Q}$ sending $z$ to $z'$ extends to an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ over $\mathbb Q$. Extend it coefficientwise to $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ while fixing $B$, then apply step 1.1 to extend it to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$. This automorphism moves $z$.

If $z$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, it is transcendental over the algebraic extension $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ by transitivity in [F2]. Extend $\{z\}$ to a transcendence basis $B$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ using [F1]. The assignment fixing $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ and every element of $B\setminus\{z\}$ while sending $z$ to $z+1$ defines an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$; its inverse sends $z$ to $z-1$. By step 1.1 it extends to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$, and it moves $z$.

Every complex number outside $\mathbb Q$ is either algebraic nonrational or transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, and steps 1.3–1.4 exhibit an automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ that moves it. Every element of $\mathbb Q$ is fixed by definition. Thus the common fixed field is exactly $\mathbb Q$.

Then contraction along $\lambda$ induces an inclusion-preserving bijection $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}R)\to\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):\mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}$. derivations.claim: Put $R=\mathbb C[M,L]$ and $S=\{M^aL^b:a,b\ge0\}$. The coordinate ring of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ is $A=S^{-1}R$, a finite-type domain with fraction field $\mathbb C(M,L)$ of transcendence degree two. Each irreducible curve $Y$ in $C$ has prime ideal $P_Y\subset A$, and its quotient coordinate ring has dimension one by [F3]. Thus [F2] gives $\dim A=2$ and $\dim(A/P_Y)=1$; [F4] yields $\operatorname{ht}(P_Y)=1$.

Contract $P_Y$ to $p_Y=P_Y\cap R$. It avoids $S$ because every element of $S$ is a unit in $A$. By [F5], contraction and extension identify all primes below $P_Y$ with primes below $p_Y$, so $p_Y$ has height one. By [F1], $p_Y=(f_Y)$ for an irreducible polynomial $f_Y\in R$. Since $p_Y$ avoids $M$ and $L$, neither variable divides $f_Y$. In the localization of the UFD $R$, an irreducible remains prime unless it divides an inverted element; therefore $f_Y/1$ is a nonunit prime and $P_Y=(f_Y/1)$.

Distinct components have distinct prime ideals, hence their irreducible generators $f_Y$ are pairwise nonassociate in the Laurent ring. A Laurent polynomial belongs to every $(f_Y)$ exactly when each pairwise nonassociate prime factor divides it; unique factorization then makes it divisible by their product. If $C$ is empty, the vanishing ideal is the unit ideal and the empty product is $F_0=1$; otherwise the same product over the components generates the vanishing ideal. In either case the generator is square-free, and any other generator differs by a Laurent unit.

By the stated rational structure, every automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ preserves the vanishing ideal. Shift the finite support of $F_0$ so its lexicographically least exponent pair is $(0,0)$, then scale its coefficient there to $1$. This gives a unique normalized generator: by [F6] any two generators differ by a Laurent unit, and the support shift and specified coefficient remove that unit. Every such field automorphism preserves the normalization, hence fixes each coefficient. By [F7] the coefficients are rational. Clearing denominators and dividing by their integer gcd gives a primitive integer Laurent polynomial. Any two primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by a Laurent unit with rational scalar part; primitivity forces that scalar to be $\pm1$.
Steps 1.1–2.2 prove existence of the square-free primitive integer equation and show that its only ambiguity is $\pm M^aL^b$.

The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

An essential smooth embedded circle in the standard torus $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ represents a nonzero primitive integral homology class. A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Two essential circles with the same primitive unoriented class are smoothly ambient isotopic. The components between disjoint essential circles have smooth annulus parameters, with prescribed product collars on their boundary circles. No choice axiom is assumed.

Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

Assume full AC. Let $A,B$ be compact connected oriented surfaces with supplied finite PL triangulations, let $\pi_1(A)\ne\{1\}$, and let $f:(A,\partial A)\to(B,\partial B)$ be a PL map inducing an injective fundamental-group map. Then $f$ is homotopic as a map of pairs either to a finite-sheeted PL covering $A\to B$, or to a map with image in $\partial B$; in the latter alternative $A$ is an annulus.

If the restriction $f|_{\partial A}$ is a local homeomorphism, the homotopy can be chosen constant on $\partial A$. The alternatives retain all orientation signs and all possible finite covering degrees; no assumption that $A$ or $B$ is closed, hyperbolic, or of negative Euler characteristic is imposed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a compact codimension-zero $C^2$ subsurface of a Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless $C^2$ surface $S$, with $C^2$ boundary. Let $G\subset\operatorname{Int}N$ be a finite embedded graph: its vertices are distinct points, each edge is a regular $C^2$ embedded arc up to its endpoints, and different edge interiors are disjoint and avoid the vertices. Closed regular edges may first be subdivided by inserting finitely many vertices. Then $N$ has a finite triangular cellulation containing $G\cup\partial N$ in its one-skeleton. Each closed triangle is an embedded topological disk, the prescribed graph and original boundary retain their regular $C^2$ arcs, and the cell maps induce a homeomorphism from a finite abstract simplicial complex onto $N$ after finite subdivision. Interior edges have two incident triangles and boundary edges one; vertex links are circles or intervals, respectively.

A cell map is required to be a homeomorphism; the statement does not assert a differentiable straightening of an arbitrary prescribed graph at its vertices. This permits tangencies between prescribed edge germs. The empty $N$ or empty $G$ is allowed.

Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.
For a CW pair $(X,A)$, the quotient cellular complex $C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)/C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(A;G)$, whose degree-$n$ group is $\bigoplus_{e^n\subseteq X\setminus A}G$, computes $H_*(X,A;G)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be the compact exterior of a smooth fibered knot, equipped with a compatible finite PL structure, and let $G$ be its connected fiber, with nonempty connected boundary. Let $S$ be a connected two-sided properly embedded incompressible finite PL surface. Suppose their boundaries have been aligned, with compatible product collars, and that there is a homeomorphism $h:S\to G$ and a homotopy from the inclusion of $S$ to the inclusion of $G$ composed with $h$, fixed on this aligned boundary through maps into $M$. Then $S$ and $G$ are ambient isotopic relative to $\partial M$. This assertion concerns the actual marked original fiber, not just existence of some fibration with fiber $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: Use [F2] to take a neat representative, preserving boundary and incompressibility. Nonseparation is preserved by its ambient topological extension. A short oriented transverse segment through $S$ closes through its connected complement to a loop intersecting $S$ once. Thus the intersection-dual cohomology class of $S$ is primitive. By [F1], $[S]=\pm[F]$ in $H_2(E_K,\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Every loop in $S$ may be represented in its interior and pushed slightly into its two-sided normal product, so its intersection with $S$ is zero. Its value under the fiber's meridian homomorphism is consequently zero. Therefore the inclusion lifts to the infinite cyclic fiber cover $\widetilde E_K=F\times\mathbb R$. The lift is an embedding, since equality of two lifted image points would imply equality of their projected points on the embedded $S$.

Align the finitely many longitude boundary curves by [F3] with distinct fiber-boundary levels in the torus, extending across its collar. In the infinite cyclic cover their lifts are horizontal circles in $\partial F\times\mathbb R$. Straighten the neat surface's smaller boundary collars to the product collars using their simultaneous half-space coordinates, fixed on the boundary curves. The projection of the lifted inclusion is now a proper map $p:(S,\partial S)\to(F,\partial F)$ equal to a product near boundary; every boundary restriction is a diffeomorphism. Its fundamental-group map is injective: the lifted inclusion is injective on fundamental groups by [F2] and covering injection, and $F\times\mathbb R\to F$ is a homotopy equivalence. The relative fundamental class of $F\times\{t\}$ generates $H_2(F\times\mathbb R,\partial F\times\mathbb R)$ and pushes to $[F]$ downstairs. Consequently $[S]=\pm[F]$ from step 1.1 makes the relative degree of $p$ equal to $\pm1$.

Give the compact smooth surfaces the finite triangulations of [F4], choosing matched boundary subdivisions through the actual boundary diffeomorphisms. On their product collars retain the boundary map and its linear collar coordinate; relatively approximate the remaining compact map by a finite PL map. Interior compact separation and sufficiently fine approximation keep it in the target interior, so this is a homotopy of pairs fixed on the original boundary. If $\pi_1S\ne1$, apply the full actual classifier [F4]. Its annular-collapse alternative induces zero on relative $H_2$, contrary to the degree $\pm1$ in step 2.1. Its finite covering alternative has absolute relative degree equal to its number of sheets, by summing the lifted oriented triangles. Thus it has one sheet and is a homeomorphism $h:S\to F$, homotopic to $p$ relative to the aligned boundary. If $\pi_1S=1$, [F5] makes $S$ a disk. Lift $p$ to the cover of $F$ for its trivial image subgroup. An infinite-sheeted cover has relative top homology zero: all coefficients of a finite two-cycle on adjacent oriented triangles agree, and connectedness forces a single coefficient on infinitely many triangles, which must vanish by finite support. A finite-sheeted cover pushes its fundamental class to its sheet number times $[F,\partial F]$. Nonzero degree $\pm1$ therefore forces this cover to have one sheet. Hence $F$ is simply connected and also a disk; its boundary map extends to a disk homeomorphism, homotopic to $p$ relative boundary by convex interpolation in disk coordinates. In either case $S$ has one boundary component. The height coordinate of its lifted inclusion can now separately be homotoped linearly to its one constant boundary height, fixed there. Combine these homotopies in $F\times\mathbb R$ and project to get an actual homotopy of the parametrized inclusion of $S$ to the corresponding fiber, relative to the aligned boundary. This asserts a homotopy of maps, not a projection of an arbitrary embedding isotopy.

The homeomorphism and actual boundary-relative homotopy in step 3.1 meet [F6]. Use [F7] on the pair cut along its transverse smooth surface faces and protected product collars, matching paired face subdivisions before regluing; this gives compatible finite structures retaining the already matched boundary triangulations. That theorem constructs an empty embedded product patch in the actual cut fiber product, verifies that the patch meets only one fiber face so embeds downstairs, and reduces the finite intersection system until the patch is the whole surface. Hence its ambient boundary-relative isotopy carries $S$ to the original marked fiber $F$. Restore the preliminary boundary-torus alignment and neatification if necessary. This proves both the isotopy assertion and its relative aligned-boundary refinement under the authorized AC assumptions.

citations.quote: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

derivations.claim: Work with the fixed finite presentation in the Statement. Fact [F1] ensures the existence of finite presentations for the knot group, but no change from the specified presentation to different Wirtinger generators is presumed here. Write each generator matrix as four coordinate variables and impose the polynomial determinant equation $\det(A_i)=1$. These finitely many equations cut out $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ in affine $4n$-space.

Evaluate each relator word by matrix multiplication, replacing each inverse letter by the adjugate matrix from [F2]. Every entry of $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)-I_2$ is therefore a polynomial in the coordinates.

A tuple in $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ satisfies all these matrix equations exactly when its generator assignment extends to a homomorphism from the presented group $G$. Hence their common zero set is precisely $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$, a closed algebraic subset of affine space.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. Let $G$ be any group and $\rho,\rho':G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ be representations with $$\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g)\qquad(g\in G).$$ If $\rho$ is irreducible, then $\rho'$ is irreducible and there is $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho'(g)=P\rho(g)P^{-1}$ for every $g$. If $\rho$ is reducible, it has the same trace character as its diagonal semisimplification $g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(\chi(g),\chi(g)^{-1})$, where $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^*$ is the character on a common invariant line. The two diagonal characters $\chi,\chi^{-1}$ determine the same semisimple conjugacy class. This is a pointwise statement; it does not assert that an irreducible character component admits a tautological representation over its function field or prove rational quotient descent.

Send $z_i$ to $t_{w_i}$. Step 1.1 makes this polynomial-ring map onto the reduced invariant coordinate algebra. Its kernel is therefore radical. The actual affine coordinate-ring construction in [F2] identifies the quotient with the closed zero locus of that kernel in $\mathbb C^N$ and its point map with the displayed trace-coordinate map. Equal listed coordinates give equal values of every element of the coordinate algebra by step 1.1. In particular they give equal traces on every group word. There are the following explicit valid finite planar codes, with the standard right/up orientation of the plane and positive based meridians using compatible common upper-collar access paths.

The counterclockwise square with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ is a crossing-free unknot code. It has one under-arc and gives $\pi_1(S^3\setminus U)=\langle x\mid\ \rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with $x$ the positive meridian.

An oriented figure-eight code has crossings $C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4$. The letters $O,U$ mean over and under, and $i,o$ mean incoming and outgoing. Its integer plane-drawing certificate is

| $r$ | $C_r$ | $rOi$ | $rOo$ | $rUi$ | $rUo$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $(-423,0)$ | $(-627,102)$ | $(-363,-30)$ | $(-363,30)$ | $(-627,-102)$ |
| $2$ | $(0,-9)$ | $(-33,-6)$ | $(99,-18)$ | $(-99,-18)$ | $(33,-6)$ |
| $3$ | $(0,9)$ | $(33,6)$ | $(-99,18)$ | $(99,18)$ | $(-33,6)$ |
| $4$ | $(423,0)$ | $(627,-102)$ | $(363,30)$ | $(363,-30)$ | $(627,102)$ |

The complete cyclic visit list is $$1O,\ 2U,\ 3O,\ 1U,\ 4O,\ 3U,\ 2O,\ 4U.$$ For every successive pair $rB,sD$ in this list, including the last-to-first pair, use the three straight segments of the route $C_r\to rBo\to sDi\to C_s$. At each crossing pair $rOi$ with $rOo$, and $rUi$ with $rUo$; the first pair is over. Smooth the degree-two bends in disjoint small disks. The cyclic orders at crossings are the counterclockwise lists $(rOo,rUi,rOi,rUo)$ for $r=1,4$ and $(rOo,rUo,rOi,rUi)$ for $r=2,3$.

Label the under-arcs $x_1:U4\to U2$, $x_2:U2\to U1$, $x_3:U1\to U3$, $x_4:U3\to U4$. In each oriented over-branch chart, let $L$ denote its left under-side (target of the positive in-plane normal), and $R$ its right under-side (source). The exact crossing table is

| crossing | over | $L$ (target) | $R$ (source) | under traversal | $\operatorname{sign}\det(\text{over},\text{under})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $R_1$ | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $x_3$ | target to source | $-1$ |
| $R_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_2$ | $x_1$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_3$ | $x_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_3$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_4$ | $x_3$ | $x_4$ | $x_1$ | target to source | $-1$ |

Thus its actual positive-meridian presentation is $$\pi_1(S^3\setminus 4_1)=\langle x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\mid x_1x_2=x_3x_1,\ x_1x_4=x_4x_2,\ x_3x_2=x_2x_4,\ x_3x_4=x_1x_3\rangle.$$ The last relation follows from the first three. Starting on $x_1$, the underpasses occur at $R_2,R_1,R_3,R_4$, and the self-writhe is zero. All drawing data, validations and algebra in this statement are finite and use no choice axiom.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Assume full AC and use the standard oriented four-crossing figure-eight code of the explicit oriented Wirtinger-code lemma, with its positive based under-arc meridians $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ and compatible diagram access paths. Put $u=x_1$, $v=x_2$, and $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$. Then $$\pi_1(E_{4_1})=\langle u,v\mid vw=wu\rangle,$$ with $u$ a positive meridian. In this presentation $$X_3=uvu^{-1},\qquad X_4=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v=w^{-1}v$$ are the old $x_3,x_4$. The preferred longitude based compatibly with $u$ is represented by $$\lambda=X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}.$$ In particular its trace in any representation is the trace of this explicit word. The formula does not identify a zero-homology centralizing word as a longitude without the diagram-parallel calculation.

Let $A,B\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ and put $a=\operatorname{tr}A$, $b=\operatorname{tr}B$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. Every word matrix in $A^{\pm1},B^{\pm1}$ is a linear combination of $I,A,B,AB$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[a,b,c]$, computed by finite word induction. Consequently its trace is a polynomial in those three traces. If $a=b=x$ and $c=y$, the coefficients specialize to $\mathbb Z[x,y]$. The assertion includes scalar, unipotent, reducible and irreducible pairs and uses no choice axiom.

Assume full AC and let $G$ be a finitely presented group. Every regular function on $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$ invariant under simultaneous conjugation is a polynomial in finitely many word-trace functions $t_w(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(w))$. Equivalently, the coordinate algebra of the affine character quotient is generated by trace functions of words in $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

derivations.claim: **Every irreducible pair has the required concrete matrix form.** Let $A=\rho(u)$ and $B=\rho(v)$. Relation $vw=wu$ makes them conjugate, hence of equal trace $x$. Choose an eigenvalue $M\ne0$ of $A$ and an eigenvector for it, and choose an eigenvector of $B$ with eigenvalue $M^{-1}$. The two lines are distinct; otherwise they form a common invariant line for the two generators. In this basis $A$ is upper triangular and $B$ is lower triangular, with respective diagonals $(M,M^{-1})$ in both cases. The upper entry of $A$ is nonzero, for otherwise the second line is common; the lower entry of $B$ is nonzero for the same reason on the first line. Rescale the second basis vector to make the upper entry of $A$ equal to one. Thus every irreducible representation is conjugate to $$A=\begin{pmatrix}M&1\\0&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}M&0\\t&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad t\ne0.$$ This works also at $M=\pm1$; no distinct-eigenvalue hypothesis was used. A scalar adjustment of the conjugating basis matrix gives determinant one if desired.

**All relator entries are computed.** Put $a=M^2+M^{-2}-3=x^2-5$ and $F=t^2+at-a$. Direct multiplication gives $$W=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}t^2+(M^2-2)t+1&M+M^{-1}(t-1)\\t\bigl(M+M^{-1}(t-1)\bigr)&1+M^{-2}t\end{pmatrix},\qquad BW-WA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-F\\tF&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Thus the representation relation is exactly $F=0$, not a condition obtained after discarding an extra entry. Conversely a pair with $F=0,t\ne0$ is irreducible. At $M=\pm1$ its two nontrivial unipotent matrices have distinct invariant lines. Otherwise a common line besides the two chosen eigenlines can occur only when $t=-(M-M^{-1})^2$; solving the two eigenvector equations gives this equality. But $F$ evaluated at that value is $1$, since $(M-M^{-1})^2=a+1$. So it never occurs on $F=0$. When $t=0$ the pair is upper triangular and reducible.

**The trace equation and its actual image.** Matrix multiplication gives $$x=M+M^{-1},\qquad y=M^2+M^{-2}+t=x^2-2+t.$$ Substituting $t=y-x^2+2$ into $F$ gives $$f(x,y)=2x^2+y^2-x^2y-y-1.$$ Every irreducible representation therefore maps to $f=0$. Conversely, if $f(x,y)=0$ and $t=y-x^2+2\ne0$, choose a root $M$ of $M^2-xM+1=0$. It is nonzero, and step 2.1 constructs an irreducible representation with those traces. The excluded points with $t=0$ have $x^2=5,y=3$, hence are only two points. In particular this is an actual dense realization of the curve, not merely a necessary trace equation.

**There is exactly one component containing irreducible characters.** The discriminant of the monic quadratic $f$ in $y$ is $$(x^2+1)^2-4(2x^2-1)=(x^2-1)(x^2-5).$$ Each of its four zeros is simple, so it is not a square in $\mathbb C(x)$: a rational square has even zero order. Thus $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C(x)$ as a quadratic in $y$, and is irreducible in $\mathbb C[x,y]$. Indeed a factor of $y$-degree zero would divide the leading coefficient one, and two positive-$y$-degree factors would give a factorization over $\mathbb C(x)$. By [F3] and [F4], $x,y$ generate the whole character algebra and give its actual closed planar model. Reducible representations have common triangular diagonal characters; the relation makes their $u,v$ diagonal characters equal, so they lie on $y=x^2-2$. Every point on this parabola is realized by the diagonal pair $A=B=\operatorname{diag}(M,M^{-1})$. Step 3.1 realizes all of $f=0$ except its two intersection points with that parabola, which are also realized diagonally. Hence the full closed character model is precisely the union of that parabola and $f=0$. The latter is the unique irreducible component containing irreducible characters, and $x$ is nonconstant on it because the monic quadratic $f(x,y)$ has a complex root for every $x$.

**The preferred word, not an unspecified centralizer element, is evaluated.** Use exactly the preferred word $C=X_4A^{-1}BX_3^{-1}$ of [F2], with $X_3=ABA^{-1}$ and $X_4=B^{-1}ABA^{-1}B$. Their matrices and the displayed $A,B$ give the Laurent polynomial identity $$\operatorname{tr}C=\bigl(M^4-M^2-2-M^{-2}+M^{-4}\bigr)+F\bigl(x^2(t+1)-tF\bigr).$$ This identity is obtained by the four indicated matrix products and the entry formula for determinant-one inverses; equivalently multiply out with $a=M^2+M^{-2}-3$ to get $\operatorname{tr}C=(x^4-5x^2+2)+F\bigl((a+5)(t+1)-tF\bigr)$. It is an identity before imposing the relator, so no denominator, exceptional parabolic point, or extra component has been canceled. On $F=0$ it gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho(\lambda)=x^4-5x^2+2$ for every irreducible representation.

Word traces are regular functions in the actual character model by [F4]. The irreducible characters are dense in the irreducible curve by steps 3.1–4.1. Consequently the longitude-trace identity of step 4.2 holds on that entire component, including its reducible intersection points. Steps 3.1–4.1 supply exactly the irreducible curve and nonconstant coordinate required in the Statement, with its original full-AC branch retained. No generic trace-model, eigenvalue-image completeness or preferred-longitude calculation remains assumed in this finite computation.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ have a finite presentation. There is a finite list of words $w_1,\ldots,w_N\in G$ whose trace functions generate the coordinate ring of $X(E_K)$, so the map $[\rho]\mapsto(\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_1),\ldots,\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_N))$ is a closed embedding into $\mathbb C^N$, with defining ideal the kernel of the induced map $\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_N]\to\mathbb C[\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2)]^{SL_2}$. On the irreducible-character locus, equal trace coordinates determine conjugate representations; on the reducible locus, the quotient records the semisimplified diagonal character, not the possibly non-diagonalizable representative.

Assume full AC. Put $T=(\mathbb C^*)^n$ and $R=\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$, with $n\ge0$. For a finite index set $B$, let $J_b$ be an ideal of $R[u_1,\ldots,u_{m_b}]$, where $m_b\ge0$, and let $X_b$ be its zero set in $T\times\mathbb C^{m_b}$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate projections of the $X_b$ to $T$. Then its Zariski closure $Z$ has radical vanishing ideal $$I(Z)=\bigcap_{b\in B}\bigl(\sqrt{J_b}\cap R\bigr).$$ Write the finite irreducible-component decomposition as $Z=\bigcup_i Z_i$, and let $C$ be the union of those $Z_i$ whose dimension is one. Then $$I(C)=\bigcap_{\dim Z_i=1}I(Z_i).$$ Thus one must select the one-dimensional components after radical elimination; the first intersection alone also retains any isolated or higher-dimensional components. Empty intersections are the unit ideal and an empty selected union is empty. If $S$ is preserved by every coordinatewise field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ (in particular, if all $J_b$ are generated by rational-coefficient Laurent polynomials), both $I(Z)$ and $I(C)$ are scalar extensions of radical ideals over $\mathbb Q$. No closedness of the projections or bound on their dimension is assumed.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite Wirtinger presentation by words in generators and their inverses, and let $\mu,\lambda$ be its marked meridian and preferred-longitude words. Let $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ consist of the pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common eigenline for $\rho(\mu)$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ with eigenvalues $M$ and $L$. Then the Zariski closure of $\mathcal E_K$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$: its radical vanishing ideal in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ is obtained by extending scalars from a radical ideal in $\mathbb Q[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $C$ be a finite union of distinct irreducible one-dimensional closed algebraic subsets of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$. Suppose its radical vanishing ideal in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ is the scalar extension of a radical ideal in $\mathbb Q[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$; this is what it means here for the reduced union to be defined over $\mathbb Q$. Then its complex vanishing ideal is generated by a square-free Laurent polynomial $F$ with primitive integer coefficients. Any two such primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: **Two finite eigenline charts.** Write the generator matrices as in [F1] and evaluate the two peripheral words by the same polynomial adjugate rule; call their matrices $U(A)$ and $V(A)$. Work over $R=\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$. In one chart put $v=(1,z)^T$ and in the other put $v=(z,1)^T$. In each impose all determinant and presented-relator equations together with the four scalar equations $U(A)v=Mv$ and $V(A)v=Lv$. These give finite ideals $J_1,J_2$ of polynomial extensions of $R$ with integer coefficients. Every common eigenline has a vector in at least one chart: divide by its first nonzero coordinate, using the second chart if its first coordinate is zero. Conversely any solution has a nonzero displayed vector and hence the required common eigenline. Their projected union is therefore exactly $\mathcal E_K$ of the definition, including repeated eigenvalues, scalar matrices and nonsemisimple peripheral matrices. No global eigenvector choice is made.

**Trace coordinates introduce no extra image.** Choose the finite words $w_j$ of [F2]. If trace coordinates are used, append variables $t_j$ and equations $t_j=\operatorname{tr}(w_j(A))$ to both charts. These right sides are integer polynomials by [F1]. Every original chart point has exactly one such trace tuple, and forgetting that tuple gives exactly the original chart; thus appending and eliminating it changes neither the projected point set nor its ideal. The eigenvalue relation is independent of the representative of a character: for irreducible representations [F2] gives conjugacy, which carries common eigenlines with their eigenvalues; for reducible representations use an invariant-line basis. The peripheral matrices are then upper triangular and commute. Their possible joint eigenvalue pairs are precisely the two diagonal pairs, with coincident pairs counted once. To verify this last assertion, if one diagonal pair differs, one of the two matrices has distinct eigenvalues; its two eigenspaces are preserved by the commuting other matrix, giving both pairs. If neither differs, all common eigenvalues are the single repeated pair, and the original invariant line supplies it. Diagonal semisimplification consequently preserves exactly these pairs. Thus quotienting creates no additional peripheral eigenvalue pairs; the matrix incidence calculation already computes the same locus.

**Radical elimination and the required selection.** Apply [F3] to the two finite charts, with the optional trace equations from step 2.1. It gives $I(\overline{\mathcal E_K})=(\sqrt{J_1}\cap R)\cap(\sqrt{J_2}\cap R)$. Decompose this closed set into its finite maximal irreducible components and retain exactly those of dimension one. Their union is exactly $V_K$ in the definition of $A_K$, so the intersection of their prime vanishing ideals is precisely $I(V_K)$. An isolated image component is not selected; no assumption that raw elimination removes it is used. The same operation discards a component of any other dimension if one occurs, without needing a separate dimension bound for the full peripheral image.

**Primitive equation.** By [F4] the point set $\mathcal E_K$ is stable under every automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$. The component-selection part of [F3] therefore gives a radical rational structure on $I(V_K)$, not merely on the ideal before selection. By [F5] its finite reduced curve union has a square-free primitive integer Laurent generator, unique up to $\pm M^aL^b$. This is $A_K$ by its defining normalization. The construction retains the full-AC branch inherited from [F2]–[F5] and makes no choice of a global eigenline section or of a closed projection image. This proves all asserted elimination and normalization claims.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime integers, choose integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $a\alpha+b\beta=1$, and put $G=\langle x,y\mid x^a=y^b\rangle$, $h=x^a=y^b$, $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$ and $\lambda=h\mu^{-ab}$. Consider all irreducible representations $\rho:G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$, where irreducible means having no common invariant complex line. The common peripheral eigenvalue pairs $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$ have reduced Zariski closure with vanishing ideal $$(1+M^{2a}L)\quad\hbox{if }b=2,\qquad (M^{2ab}L^2-1)\quad\hbox{if }b>2.$$ More precisely, $\rho(h)=\epsilon I$ with $\epsilon=-1$ when $b=2$ and $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ when $b>2$; each permitted sign occurs in a family realizing every point of the graph $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$ except possibly finitely many meridian values. The displayed ideal is the ideal of the entire irreducible eigenvalue locus, not just of the exhibited families. No choice axiom is assumed.

There are the following explicit valid finite planar codes, with the standard right/up orientation of the plane and positive based meridians using compatible common upper-collar access paths.

The counterclockwise square with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ is a crossing-free unknot code. It has one under-arc and gives $\pi_1(S^3\setminus U)=\langle x\mid\ \rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with $x$ the positive meridian.

An oriented figure-eight code has crossings $C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4$. The letters $O,U$ mean over and under, and $i,o$ mean incoming and outgoing. Its integer plane-drawing certificate is

| $r$ | $C_r$ | $rOi$ | $rOo$ | $rUi$ | $rUo$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be finitely presented, let its reduced complex $SL_2$ representation variety have its trace-coordinate affine character quotient, and let $X$ be a nonempty irreducible closed subset of that quotient containing an irreducible character. Write $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. There is a field $L/K$ of degree at most two and an absolutely irreducible representation $\sigma:G\to SL_2(L)$ whose every word trace is the corresponding function on $X$.

More precisely, for some $0\ne f\in A$ there is a subring $B\subset L$ which is either $A_f$ or the free rank-two algebra $A_f[\xi]=A_f[T]/(T^2-aT+1)$, where $a$ is one word trace and $a^2-4$ is a unit. All generator matrices lie in $SL_2(B)$. Every $\chi\in D_X(f)$ admits a homomorphism $B\to\mathbb C$ extending evaluation at $\chi$; every resulting representation has character $\chi$ and is irreducible. This is an actual family of representatives, not merely agreement of formal traces. One can enlarge $f$ to make any specified finite list of nonzero elements of $L$ and their inverses belong to $B$.

If $[L:K]=2$, its nonidentity automorphism $\tau$ acts on $\sigma$ by simultaneous conjugation with an explicit matrix $P\in GL_2(L)$. Consequently any projective point obtained from $\sigma$ by finite field operations that commute with field automorphisms and whose value is invariant under simultaneous $GL_2$ conjugation is defined over $K$. This clause presumes that the construction is actually defined and invariant; it supplies no homological rank, tangent-space or essential-surface assertion.

Assume full AC. Let $(Y,y)$ be a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected based space, and fix an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle\ \cong\ \Gamma=\pi_1(Y,y)$$
from a finite presentation. Let $P$ be its presentation $2$-complex, with its one vertex $p$. Choose based loops in $Y$ representing the specified generators. They extend, after choosing fillings of the finitely many relators, to a based map $f:P\to Y$ inducing the specified isomorphism. No CW structure on $Y$ is required. For every left $\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$-module $A$, interpreted as the base fibre of a local system with $g a=T_{\bar g}a$ in the first-loop-first convention, this map induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(P;f^*\mathcal A)\ \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\ H_1(Y;\mathcal A).$$
This assertion does not require $Y$ or its universal cover to be aspherical and does not assert that $P$ is a spine or a homotopy-equivalent model of $Y$.

There is the following explicit finite-chain form. Give universal-cover chains the right action $c\cdot g=T_{g^{-1}}c$, and choose the lifted presentation vertex $e_0$ and generator edges $e_j$ starting there. For a word $w$ in the generators and their inverses, let each positive letter $x_j$ after prefix $q$ contribute $e_j\cdot q^{-1}$, and each negative letter $x_j^{-1}$ after prefix $q$ contribute $-e_j\cdot(qx_j^{-1})^{-1}$. Denote the sum by $c_w$. Then
$$\partial c_w=e_0\cdot w^{-1}-e_0.$$
If $u\in A$ is fixed by $w$, the tensor $c_w\otimes u$ is a cycle. Under the displayed isomorphism its class is the class of the actual based loop in $Y$ represented by $w$, with initial coefficient $u$; it is independent of the word representative and the relator fillings of $f$.

In particular let $j:(T^2,*)\to(Y,y)$ be a based torus map with ordered based loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, choose words $w_\lambda,w_\mu$ for their images, and let $u$ be fixed by both. The two finite cycles $c_{w_\lambda}\otimes u,c_{w_\mu}\otimes u$ compute the images of the actual torus classes in precisely this order. If $A$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $F$, the presentation complex gives finite matrices $B:C_2\to C_1$, $C:C_1\to C_0$ and these two cycle columns $U$, with $CB=CU=0$. The actual kernel of the two peripheral classes mapping into $H_1(Y;\mathcal A)$ is exactly
$$\ker\{F^2\xrightarrow{U}\ker C/\operatorname{im}B\}.$$
Thus a one-dimensional image of those two actual peripheral classes is equivalent to $\operatorname{rank}_F(B\mid U)=\operatorname{rank}_FB+1$. All matrix entries are finite sums of matrices for generator words and their inverses. For the left coefficient action $\operatorname{Ad}\rho$ of an $SL_2$ representation they are polynomial in the representation entries and in the chosen vector $u$. For a torus restriction with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))^2\ne4$, one may take $u=\rho(\mu)-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))I$ in characteristic different from $2$; the two torus classes are then a basis. This applies, in particular, to an actual compact smooth knot exterior and its based peripheral torus map. No existence of a generic representation family or generic exterior rank is inferred.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic different from $2$, and let $L,M\in SL_2(F)$ commute. Write $t=\operatorname{tr}M$ and suppose $\Delta=t^2-4\ne0$. Give the torus $T^2$ an ordered pair of based oriented generating loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, and give its adjoint local system intrinsic monodromies $P=\operatorname{Ad}L$ and $Q=\operatorname{Ad}M$ on $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(F)$. Here monodromy acts on column coefficient vectors on the left. Set
$$v=M-\frac t2 I,\qquad W=\{X\in V:\operatorname{tr}(vX)=0\}.$$
Then $V=Fv\oplus W$, both summands are preserved by $P,Q$, and $P,Q$ are the identity on $Fv$. There is an explicit split chain model
$$0\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow{d_2}V\oplus V\xrightarrow{d_1}V\longrightarrow0,$$
where $d_2z=((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$ and $d_1(x,y)=(P-I)x+(Q-I)y$, in the ordered edge coordinates $(\lambda,\mu)$. Its $W$ subcomplex is contractible, so
$$H_0(T^2;V)=F[v],\qquad H_1(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes\lambda]\oplus F[v\otimes\mu],\qquad H_2(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes[T^2]].$$
In particular the two displayed peripheral classes are an actual basis, without imposing any norm-one normalization on $v$. The splitting, contraction and classes commute with field extensions and simultaneous conjugation of $L,M$. All their matrix entries are rational expressions in the entries of $L,M$, with denominators powers of $2$ and $\Delta$. This assertion concerns boundary-torus homology only: it makes no claim about the rank of its inclusion into the homology of a knot exterior.

Let $A$ be a commutative integral domain with fraction field $F$. Let $B:A^s\to A^n$, $C:A^n\to A^t$ and $U=(u,v):A^2\to A^n$ be finite matrices with $CB=CU=0$. Put $\beta=\operatorname{rank}_F B$, $\gamma=\operatorname{rank}_F C$, and assume $$\operatorname{rank}_F(B\mid U)=\beta+1.$$ Then $h=n-\gamma-\beta\ge1$. There exists $0\ne f\in A$ such that, over $A_f$, the kernel, image and homology $H_f=\ker C_f/\operatorname{im}B_f$ have explicit free bases, with ranks $n-\gamma$, $\beta$ and $h$. The kernel $$L_f=\ker\{A_f^2\xrightarrow{U_f}H_f\}$$ is a free rank-one direct summand of $A_f^2$. In explicit homology coordinates the images of $u,v$ can be written $a e_1,b e_1$, with at least one of $a,b$ a unit of $A_f$. Hence $$L_f=A_f(-b,a).$$ All these assertions, including the displayed kernel, commute with any homomorphism $A_f\to E$ to a field. In particular they describe the actual homology kernel of the specialized matrices, not just a kernel before specialization.

If $A=\mathbb C[X]$ for a nonempty irreducible affine algebraic set $X$, this gives a regular projective kernel line $[-b:a]$ on a nonempty dense principal open subset and hence a rational map $X\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1$. Its slope convention $-\text{second coordinate}/\text{first coordinate}$ is the projective value $[a:b]$, including zero and infinity. The rank-chart expressions agree wherever both are defined. The kernel line is unchanged by invertible changes of the three chain bases, by adding boundary columns to $U$, and by multiplying both columns of $U$ by the same invertible scalar. For rational changes it is unchanged after restricting to a common open set where their denominators and inverses are defined. No assertion that the matrix rank hypotheses hold for an arbitrary topological or representation-theoretic family is part of this lemma.

Let $G$ be any group and $\rho,\rho':G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ be representations with $$\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g)\qquad(g\in G).$$ If $\rho$ is irreducible, then $\rho'$ is irreducible and there is $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho'(g)=P\rho(g)P^{-1}$ for every $g$. If $\rho$ is reducible, it has the same trace character as its diagonal semisimplification $g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(\chi(g),\chi(g)^{-1})$, where $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^*$ is the character on a common invariant line. The two diagonal characters $\chi,\chi^{-1}$ determine the same semisimple conjugacy class. This is a pointwise statement; it does not assert that an irreducible character component admits a tautological representation over its function field or prove rational quotient descent.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ have admissible adjoint local system, and let $v_\rho$ be a nonzero peripheral-adjoint-invariant vector for which $[v_\rho\otimes\lambda],[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$ form the specified ordered basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$. If a generator of the one-dimensional kernel of inclusion is $a[v_\rho\otimes\lambda]+b[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$, the **Bénard–Florens–Rodau slope** is $s_K(\rho)=-b/a\in\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$, with $a=0$ interpreted as $\infty$. Rescaling $v_\rho$ or the kernel generator does not change this projective ratio. A rational function on an irreducible character component means an element of its function field, the fraction field of its coordinate domain. A projective-valued rational function means a point of the projective line over that field; it may be identically $\infty$. The slope's rational extension has this projective meaning. Unless its generic value is $\infty$, it is an ordinary rational function, whose individual infinite values are poles. Its rational extension is not a value assigned to every singular or inadmissible character.

Let $A,B\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ commute. There is a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$ invariant under both $A$ and $B$. Equivalently, in a basis beginning with a nonzero vector in that subspace, both matrices are upper triangular.

derivations.claim: **Conjugation and the actual peripheral basis.** Simultaneous conjugation by an invertible matrix sends each coefficient vector to its conjugate and intertwines every intrinsic path transport. It therefore is an isomorphism of the actual local coefficient complexes and carries the ordered peripheral cycles and their inclusion kernel to the corresponding ones. Rescaling their common invariant vector rescales both columns and leaves that kernel in the two prescribed coordinates unchanged. Thus the slope is conjugation invariant wherever its given admissible definition applies. For a non-boundary-parabolic torus pair, at least one of the longitude and meridian matrices has trace squared different from four: if both traces squared were four, simultaneous triangularization of the commuting pair would give diagonal eigenvalues in $\{1,-1\}$, and the same would hold for every peripheral word, the boundary-parabolic case. Choose one such loop $\delta$. If $\delta$ is the longitude, apply [F3] with the two torus generators interchanged and then restore the ordered (longitude,meridian) coordinates. In either case $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\delta))I/2$ is nonzero and its two named classes are an actual basis. The common fixed coefficient space is exactly the line spanned by $u$, by the complementary-plane contraction in [F3]; hence every admissible choice of common vector gives this same ordered kernel.

**An actual generic family on the component.** Put $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Apply [F1] to obtain $\sigma$ over $L$, with $[L:K]\le2$, and its spreading ring $B$ over a principal localization of $A$. The proof of [F1] also gives a nonempty open irreducible-character certificate on $X$. Intersect it with the supplied dense admissible open; this is nonempty because $X$ is irreducible. At a point of this intersection choose $\delta$ as in step1.1. Its discriminant is then a nonzero regular function on $X$, so enlarge the localization to invert it. All generic matrices and $u$ are now in $B$, and every point of this principal open has an actual irreducible representative obtained by specialization. No representation over $K$ itself, nor any abstract rational quotient descent, is being assumed.

**Verify the geometric rank hypothesis before invoking a kernel chart.** Use [F2] with the actual exterior and its fixed finite presentation and peripheral words. Over $B$ this gives finite matrices $D_2,D_1$ and $U=(u_\lambda,u_\mu)$ satisfying $D_1D_2=D_1U=0$; these identities hold because they hold over the field $L$ and $B$ injects into $L$. Let $\beta=\operatorname{rank}_L D_2$ and $r=\operatorname{rank}_L(D_2\mid U)$. Finite Gaussian elimination over $L$ provides invertible row and column transformations taking each of these two matrices to its identity-plus-zero block form. Clear the finitely many nonzero denominators of all entries of these transformations and their inverse matrices. Zero entries require no inversion. The norm argument in [F1] realizes all these inversions by shrinking the principal open in $X$. The block identities then hold in $B$ and persist under every specialization $B\to\mathbb C$; hence both ranks are respectively $\beta$ and $r$ at every such specialization. The principal open meets the supplied dense admissible locus. At a point of that intersection, [F2] identifies the quotient images of $U$ with the actual peripheral inclusion, and step1.1 identifies its domain with the actual two-dimensional torus homology. Admissibility says its kernel has dimension one, so its image has dimension one. Thus $r-\beta=1$. This proves the generic rank hypothesis from the given actual geometric locus, rather than postulating it for an abstract matrix family.

**Construct the algebraic homology line with actual specializations.** Apply [F4] to the domain $B$ and its fraction field $L$, taking its matrices $B,C$ there to be $D_2,D_1$ here. Step3.1 supplies exactly its rank-one hypothesis. After a finite localization it gives explicit split bases for cycles, boundaries and homology and a kernel line generated by $(-b,a)$, with one of $a,b$ invertible and quotient images of the two $U$ columns equal to $a e_1,b e_1$. Once again [F1] converts this finite localization to one principal localization of $A$. Every complex specialization now computes the actual specialized homology and kernel, by [F4], and [F2] identifies them with the actual exterior and ordered peripheral inclusion. The slope is therefore $[a:b]$, since applying minus the second coordinate divided by the first to $[-b:a]$ gives $a/b$. Zero and infinity are retained. This also supplies the requested constant-rank homology bundles on this finite covering open, rather than relying on a possibly nonalgebraic unit-vector choice.

**Descend the constructed line to the character field.** The matrix construction commutes with field automorphisms: all word actions, boundaries and $u$ use polynomial operations and rational constants. Under simultaneous conjugation, the invertible map $\operatorname{Ad}(P)$ intertwines the coefficient matrices and sends $u$ to its new value, so carries their actual homology quotient and peripheral map to the corresponding ones, without changing the two input coordinates. Thus its kernel line, and hence $[a:b]$, is invariant. In the quadratic case [F1] supplies $\tau(\sigma)=P\sigma P^{-1}$; the same compatibility shows $\tau[a:b]=[a:b]$. The explicit projective descent in [F1] places that point in $\mathbb P^1(K)$. In the degree-one case it already lies there. This is descent of an explicitly constructed rational line, not the inference that pointwise conjugacy alone implies rationality.

**Identify the rational extension with the slope.** Normalize a nonzero homogeneous coordinate of this $K$-point to one and clear its finitely many $A$ denominators. Shrinking once more also makes its equality with the $B$ rank-chart line an equality at every specialized point. Its coordinates define a rational map $X\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1$, regular on this nonempty dense principal open. At every point there in the original admissible locus, step4.1 gives its actual BFR slope. Every irreducible representative with that character is conjugate to the specialized representative by [F5], and step1.1 gives identical values. Choices of words, pivots, model or shrinking yield the same rational map: both maps agree with the actual slope on the intersection with the dense given locus; cross multiplication of their rational homogeneous coordinates then vanishes on a dense set, and hence vanishes in the coordinate domain. Thus the generically defined slope has the asserted rational extension. For a one-dimensional $X$ the same homogeneous coordinates give a point of $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C(X))$. If its second coordinate is nonzero, their quotient belongs to $\mathbb C(X)$ and gives the ordinary rational function, allowing poles at individual points. If its second coordinate is zero, it is the identically infinite projective function. No generic finiteness assertion is made, and no value at a singular or inadmissible point is assigned by this proof. The scheme-smooth condition is retained as supplied; the finite-rank argument needs no stronger interpretation of it and imports no tangent-space theorem. This proves the full stated rationality and conjugation assertions, independently of the logarithmic Gauss or ideal-point theorems.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this

([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with exterior $E_K$, positive meridian $\mu$, and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Define $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ to consist of all pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common invariant line on which $\rho(\mu)$ acts by $M$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ acts by $L$. The Zariski closure is the smallest Zariski-closed algebraic subset containing $\mathcal E_K$; let $V_K$ be the union of its one-dimensional irreducible components, where an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. Zero-dimensional image components are omitted. The **ordinary A-polynomial** $A_K(M,L)$ is the Laurent polynomial generating the vanishing ideal of $V_K$, chosen square-free (no repeated irreducible factors) and with primitive integer coefficients (their greatest common divisor is one). It is determined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$ for $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. Its reduced curve includes the abelian component $L=1$; equivalently, its representative in $\mathbb Z[M,L]$ is divisible by $L-1$.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. The restriction of representations of $\pi_1(E_K)$ to the peripheral torus gives an eigenvalue locus in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ with algebraic Zariski closure. Its one-dimensional reduced image components are exactly the curve components used in $A_K(M,L)$; isolated image points contribute no curve factor. Radical elimination of the representation, trace and eigenline coordinates from the finite presentation incidence equations, followed by retaining precisely the one-dimensional irreducible components, yields the Laurent ideal of that curve union, whose square-free primitive generator is $A_K$ up to $\pm M^aL^b$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

A smooth collar is a smooth embedding $c:\partial M\times[0,\varepsilon)\to M$ such that $c(p,0)=p$ and whose image is an open neighbourhood of $\partial M$ in $M$. Locally one may first use a positive smooth width depending on $p$.

derivations.claim: Inclusion of the boundary torus into the exterior gives a homomorphism of fundamental groups. Precomposing a representation with this homomorphism is polynomial in matrix entries, so it is a regular map of representation varieties and is equivariant for simultaneous conjugation.

Pullback along this equivariant map sends conjugation-invariant regular functions to conjugation-invariant regular functions, hence induces the algebraic restriction morphism on affine categorical quotients.

By [F2], the defining equation of the reduced curve union vanishes on each of its one-dimensional image components. The definition takes only those components, so an isolated image point outside their union is not added as a curve factor.

Write the attached solid torus as $V=D^2\times S^1$, let $A=\{0\}\times S^1$, and base at $(0,1)$. The retraction $r(z,w)=(0,w)$ and inclusion $i:A\hookrightarrow V$ satisfy $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_A$, and the homotopy $((z,w),t)\mapsto((1-t)z,w)$ from $\operatorname{id}_V$ to $i\circ r$ fixes the basepoint. By [F5] and [F6], $\pi_1(V,(0,1))\cong\pi_1(S^1,1)\cong\mathbb Z$.

By [A1] and [F7], the exterior boundary has a collar; $V$ has its product collar. Thickening the two pieces across opposite halves of the gluing collar gives an open cover of the filled manifold whose sets retract to $E_K$ and $V$ and whose intersection retracts to the torus. These spaces are path connected, so [F4] identifies the filled fundamental group as their pushout.

Since $\mu,\lambda$ commute, the primitive class $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ is represented by $\mu^p\lambda^q$. It maps to the identity in $\pi_1(V)$ because it is the meridian. Complete $(p,q)$ to a unimodular basis of $\mathbb Z^2$ by Bézout; the complementary class has longitude coefficient $\pm1$ on $\partial V$, hence maps to a generator of $\pi_1(V)$ by step 2.1. The pushout from step 2.2 identifies this generator with the image of the complementary class in $\pi_1(E_K)$ and imposes only the relation $\mu^p\lambda^q=1$. Eliminating the generator gives $\pi_1(E_K(p/q))\cong\pi_1(E_K)/\langle\!\langle\mu^p\lambda^q\rangle\!\rangle$.

A homomorphism from this quotient is exactly a homomorphism from $\pi_1(E_K)$ that kills $\mu^p\lambda^q$. Since $\rho(\mu)$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ commute, this condition is the matrix equation $\rho(\mu)^p\rho(\lambda)^q=I_2$.

If the two peripheral matrices are simultaneously diagonalized, their product of powers is $\operatorname{diag}(M^pL^q,(M^pL^q)^{-1})$, which is the identity exactly when $M^pL^q=1$. For a merely triangular pair, the diagonal entries still give this necessary equation, but they do not determine the off-diagonal entries of the product; the matrix relation remains the exact test.
