Assume full AC and let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime positive integers. With the meridian-longitude and exponent conventions used for the enhanced A-polynomial, the enhanced A-polynomial of $T_{a,b}$ is, up to multiplication by a Laurent unit,
$$\widetilde A_{T_{a,b}}(M,L)=\begin{cases}1+M^{2a}L,&b=2,\\-1+M^{2ab}L^2,&b>2.\end{cases}$$
If $K$ is the unknot, then $\widetilde A_K=1$. The nontrivial torus-knot Newton polygon is therefore a line segment whose slope in the $(a,b)\mapsto M^bL^a$ convention is $ab$.

Let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime integers, choose integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $a\alpha+b\beta=1$, and put $G=\langle x,y\mid x^a=y^b\rangle$, $h=x^a=y^b$, $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$ and $\lambda=h\mu^{-ab}$. Consider all irreducible representations $\rho:G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$, where irreducible means having no common invariant complex line. The common peripheral eigenvalue pairs $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$ have reduced Zariski closure with vanishing ideal $$(1+M^{2a}L)\quad\hbox{if }b=2,\qquad (M^{2ab}L^2-1)\quad\hbox{if }b>2.$$ More precisely, $\rho(h)=\epsilon I$ with $\epsilon=-1$ when $b=2$ and $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ when $b>2$; each permitted sign occurs in a family realizing every point of the graph $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$ except possibly finitely many meridian values. The displayed ideal is the ideal of the entire irreducible eigenvalue locus, not just of the exhibited families. No choice axiom is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the standard oriented three-sphere with $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and choose $0<r<1$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $p,q$ are coprime nonzero integers and $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, then the oriented torus knot $T(p,q)$ is ambient isotopic in $S^3$ to the standard unknot with its standard orientation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with one torus cusp and a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. In a neighborhood of its complete holonomy, the representation deformation space modulo conjugacy is a complex one-dimensional manifold, with local coordinate $s=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu)$ near $s=4$ for a chosen peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$.

Augment a representation by choosing a common invariant line of its peripheral holonomy. The augmented deformation space is a smooth complex curve, with holomorphic eigenvalue-ratio logarithm coordinate $u$ vanishing at the complete point. The forgetful map to the ordinary conjugacy quotient is $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$. The corresponding logarithm $v(u)$ for $\lambda$ satisfies $v(0)=0$ and $v(u)=\tau u+O(u^2)$. Here $\operatorname{Im}\tau\ne0$; it is positive for a positively oriented basis of the oriented horotorus, and changes sign if the basis orientation is reversed. In particular the eigenvalue logarithm is a coordinate on the augmented space, rather than a single-valued holomorphic coordinate on the ordinary quotient.

The pair $(u,v)$ records the local generalized filling parameters. The primitive slope equation $p u+q v(u)=2\pi i$ has its full-turn holonomy meaning for ordinary smooth filling when $\gcd(p,q)=1$; sufficiently large primitive coefficients admit such small solutions and smooth complete hyperbolic fillings. Nonprimitive ray parameters are not ordinary slopes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. The **enhanced A-polynomial** $\widetilde A_K(M,L)$ is the primitive square-free Laurent polynomial defining the union of one-dimensional peripheral-eigenvalue image components arising from irreducible characters of $\pi_1(E_K)$. It is defined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$. The ordinary A-polynomial is the least common multiple $A_K=\operatorname{lcm}(\widetilde A_K,L-1)$, up to a Laurent unit, where the least common multiple uses each distinct irreducible Laurent factor only once; the factor $L-1$ is the contribution of the abelian character component, and an irreducible component may also contribute that same factor.

Assume full AC. Let $E$ be the compact exterior of a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Let $X$ be an irreducible one-dimensional component of its complex $SL_2$ character variety. Fix a one-dimensional peripheral eigenvalue-image component $Y$ arising from $X$, with coordinates $(M,L)$ ordered as (meridian,longitude), and an irreducible Laurent equation $P(M,L)=0$ for $Y$. Write $K=\mathbb C(X)$.

There is a finite extension $F/K$ with an actual generic representation $\rho:\pi_1(E)\to SL_2(F)$ and a choice of common peripheral eigenline whose eigenvalues are $M,L\in F^*$. These give the specified generic point of $Y$. Its actual intrinsic adjoint peripheral homology has a two-dimensional boundary basis ordered (longitude,meridian) and a one-dimensional inclusion kernel. With $\delta\in\{\lambda,\mu\}$ having distinct peripheral eigenvalues, set $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\delta))I/2$. In that basis its kernel is exactly
$$\ker\left\{F^2\longrightarrow\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C},\quad (a,b)\longmapsto a\,\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}+b\,\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right\}.$$
The two displayed differentials are not both zero. Thus its projective slope, with convention $s=-b/a$ for the kernel line, is
$$s=\left[\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}:\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right]=[-M P_M:L P_L]\ \in\mathbb P^1(F).$$
A ratio of one-forms here means their coordinate pair in any nonzero basis of the one-dimensional $F$-space $\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C}$. The result is independent of that basis, the finite field model, the common eigenline and simultaneous conjugation, and is defined over $K$. It includes zero when $\mathrm dL=0$ and infinity when $\mathrm dM=0$. In particular a nonconstant meridian eigenvalue is not assumed.

This is an identity of rational projective maps. It agrees with the actual specialized homology slope on a nonempty dense rank-chart open. At every point where the rational extension and the peripheral restriction are evaluated and $(P_M,P_L)\ne(0,0)$, its projective value is $[-M P_M:L P_L]$; when $P_L\ne0$ this is the ordinary value $-M P_M/(L P_L)$. For the square-free ordinary A-polynomial, replacing $P$ by the full polynomial gives the same ratio at a point where its gradient is nonzero. No assertion that all specialized exterior homology ranks are constant outside that open, nor any ideal-point tree or essential-surface construction, is part of this lemma.

Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Then
$$ \dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Noetherian
topological space ([[def-noetherian-topological-space]]) and let irreducible
components be those of [[def-irreducible-component-of-a-topological-space]]. Then
$X$ is a finite union of irreducible closed subsets of $X$, and consequently $X$
has only finitely many irreducible components.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$, and put $a=|p|$, $b=|q|$. For $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, define
$$\delta_{a,b}(t)=\frac{(t^{ab}-1)(t-1)}{(t^a-1)(t^b-1)}.$$
Then $\delta_{a,b}(t)$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb Z[t]$, the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$ defined as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the positive-meridian infinite-cyclic-cover module satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\delta_{a,b}(t)$, and the knot genus is $g(K)=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. Here $f\doteq g$ means $f=\pm t^k g$ for some integer $k$.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot and let $A(M,L)$ be its reduced ordinary or enhanced A-polynomial, with exponent point $(a,b)$ representing $L^aM^b$. For every one-dimensional Newton face, every nonzero complex root of its edge polynomial in a primitive edge coordinate is a root of unity. This includes the entire Newton segment when the Newton polygon has dimension one. The assertion is vacuous for a constant polynomial.

More precisely, let $(u,v)$ be a primitive integral minimum normal to the face and put $y=L^{-v}M^u$. After dividing the face polynomial by a Laurent monomial and a nonzero scalar, regard it as a polynomial in $y$ with nonzero constant term. For each of its roots $c\in\mathbb C^*$ there is an integer $d>0$ such that $c^{2d}=1$.

Consequently, if the Newton support is contained in an integral line of primitive direction $(q,p)$, every one-dimensional irreducible peripheral graph $M^pL^q=c$ contributing to $A$ has a root of unity as its constant. No nonzero condition on $q$ is asserted or inferred by this conclusion.

Assume full AC. Let a smooth fibered satellite knot be written $K=P(C)$ with essential companion torus $T$, nontrivial companion $C$, and pattern not isotopic to the core of its solid torus. Let $w$ be its signed winding number. Then $w\ne0$ and
$$g(K)=g(P(U))+|w|g(C).$$
More precisely, a product decomposition obtained by cutting the given fiber produces connected-surface mapping-torus descriptions of the companion and pattern-closure exteriors, with fiber surfaces of their minimal Seifert genera. If the symmetric Alexander polynomial of $K$ has nonzero coefficients in both its highest degree and the immediately next degree, then $P(U)$ is nontrivial. No instanton theorem is assumed or proved by this assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume full AC. Let $P\subset V=S^1\times D^2$ be an oriented smooth pattern of signed winding $w$, let $C\subset S^3$ be an oriented smooth companion, and form $K=P(C)$ by the specified zero-framed oriented tubular embedding. Let $P(U)$ denote its closure under the zero-framed unknotted embedding of the same product solid torus. Write $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$, with outer product marking $(\mu_V,\lambda_V)$. On its inner torus use $(\mu_P,\lambda_P)$, where $\lambda_P$ is the preferred longitude of $P(U)$. Then
$$H_1(X_P;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_P]\oplus\mathbb Z[\lambda_V],\qquad [\mu_V]=w[\mu_P],\qquad [\lambda_P]=w[\lambda_V].$$
The inner marking becomes exactly the preferred marking $(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$ after satellite gluing. Compatible access paths are retained; arbitrary changes conjugate the corresponding group restrictions and do not change these homology or eigenvalue assertions.

Every irreducible representation of $\pi_1(E_{P(U)})$ extends, after restriction to $X_P$, to an irreducible representation of $\pi_1(E_K)$ with the identical inner peripheral eigenvalues. For $w\ne0$, every one-dimensional irreducible-character peripheral image curve of $C$ has a finite function-field cover carrying an actual irreducible satellite representation whose eigenvalues satisfy
$$M_K^w=M_C,\qquad L_K=L_C^w.$$
Here the common peripheral eigenline is part of the data. No pointwise simultaneous diagonalization at parabolic exceptional points is asserted.

In particular, suppose the enhanced polynomial of $K$ has support on a line of primitive direction $(q,p)$, where the exponent pair $(a,b)$ denotes $L^aM^b$. Then the enhanced polynomial of $P(U)$ has support on a line of the same direction. If $w\ne0$, the enhanced polynomial of $C$ has support on a line of direction $(q w^2,p)$, reduced to a primitive vector when necessary. Unit enhanced polynomials, with one-point support, are included. Thus for a finite slope $r=p/q$, $q\ne0$, pattern closure is $r$-thin and companion is $(r/w^2)$-thin. No assertion that $w\ne0$, that $P(U)$ is nontrivial, or that any knot is fibered or an instanton L-space knot is made here.

Assume full AC. If the chosen exterior of a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ has a smooth Seifert fibration, then $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphisms to a coprime torus knot or to the unknot. No atoroidality hypothesis is needed. The underlying Seifert base is a disk with at most two exceptional points. With zero or one exceptional point the exterior is a solid torus and $K$ is the unknot; with two exceptional multiplicities $q_1,q_2$, these are coprime and are the absolute parameters of the resulting torus knot, up to interchange. The assertion uses the actual meridian filling of the knot exterior, not a classification of arbitrary Seifert-fibered closed three-manifolds.

Assume full AC. Every smooth embedded torus in $S^3$ has a side whose closure is a parametrized smooth solid torus. If both sides are solid tori, there is an orientation-preserving smooth ambient isotopy taking this torus to a standard Clifford torus. Consequently every essential smooth circle on it is a torus knot or the unknot, through actual smooth ambient isotopies, not merely through an unspecified diffeomorphism of $S^3$.

If $T$ is an essential smooth torus in the interior of a chosen smooth knot exterior $E_K$, the side containing the knot tube is a parametrized solid torus $V$. It has a nontrivial smooth core knot $C$ and an orientation-preserving parameter $e:S^1\times D^2\to V$ identifying the positive meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $C$. The pattern $P=e^{-1}(K)$, with its pulled-back tube, gives the actual equality $K=P(C)$ and the actual exterior gluing along $T$. The pattern is not isotopic to the core in the solid torus. In particular this conclusion retains the actual essential companion torus and its meridian/longitude marking. No winding-nonzero assertion is imposed on a general satellite.

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a knot. The input package required by the Baldwin–Sivek thin-knot and infinitely-many-abelian-surgeries arguments consists of the following conclusions with their stated hypotheses: (i) a nontrivial $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-averse knot has a unique rational accumulation slope and either it or its mirror is an instanton L-space knot; (ii) a nontrivial instanton L-space knot is fibered and its symmetrized Alexander polynomial has coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ with nonzero coefficients alternating in sign; (iii) the L-space satellite restrictions and the pattern/companion surgery-transfer statements exclude the satellite cases used in §§3–5; and (iv) the hyperbolic Dehn-filling theorem and the knot-exterior JSJ classification reduce the remaining cases to torus knots. This carrier records the exact imported result interfaces and does not assert that these conclusions have been proved locally.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E_K$ be the compact connected orientable exterior of a smooth knot in $S^3$, with one torus boundary component. If $E_K$ is irreducible, its boundary is incompressible, $E_K$ is atoroidal, and $E_K$ is not Seifert-fibered, then $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ admits a complete finite-volume Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ with one torus cusp. No conclusion is asserted for a torus or satellite knot unless its exterior satisfies all four topological hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The unknot and all positive nontrivial torus knots are thin by [F1]: their enhanced curves have respectively the unit equation and the two explicitly calculated monomial terms. These are actual proved formulas, rather than assumptions on an uncomputed torus character variety.

This proves the forward direction for every signed torus knot as well. Reflection carries its oriented meridian to the inverse positive meridian of the reflected knot: it preserves the carried knot orientation and reverses the ambient normal-plane orientation. It carries its preferred longitude to the preferred longitude, because the degree along the knot remains one and its exterior homology class remains zero; uniqueness in [F3] excludes any meridian shift. Composition of representations with this exterior diffeomorphism therefore identifies the peripheral loci by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L)$, preserving irreducibility and all closure dimensions. Their reduced curve equations differ by that Laurent substitution and a unit. Reversing the knot orientation instead inverts both peripheral generators and gives $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. These invertible integral changes of exponents preserve containment in an affine line. Finally swapping the two complex coordinates of the standard $S^3$ interchanges the two torus parameters and preserves ambient orientation; the radial torus parameter may be changed by a smooth radial isotopy. Thus, using the mirror and orientation conventions in [F1], every coprime torus knot reduces to the positive case, or to the unknot if one parameter has absolute value one. In the latter case the actual sine-cosine circle isotopy and ambient extension in the unit-slope supplier [F1] give the unknot, with its countable-choice hypothesis supplied by full AC. This is a proof of thinness for mirrors, not an assertion that the displayed positive formula applies unchanged to a negative knot.

Suppose now that the knot exterior has the complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. We first construct the necessary SL2 lift on this EXTERIOR; no lift of the holonomy of a closed filling is assumed. Alexander duality in [F3], in degrees one and two, gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2(E_K;\mathbb Z)=0$, since the knot is a connected circle. The universal coefficient exact sequence therefore gives $H^2(E_K;\mathbb Z/2)=0$. On a finite triangulation choose a spanning tree and the associated finitely many vertex base paths. A PSL2 representation labels each oriented edge by its based transport; the labels multiply to identity around every triangle. Lift each edge label to SL2, choosing the reverse lift as its inverse. A triangle product is a central sign. The four triangle signs around each tetrahedron sum to zero in $\mathbb Z/2$: after conjugating to one vertex the intermediate edge factors cancel and the remaining signs commute. They are therefore a simplicial two-cocycle. Its cohomology class is zero, so it is the coboundary of a one-cochain. Multiply each edge lift by its corresponding sign. Every triangle product is now identity, and edge-path homotopy gives an actual SL2 representation lifting the specified PSL2 one. This finite argument uses the space cohomology directly and inserts no spin or closed-three-manifold parallelizability theorem.

The lift works for the local holonomy family, not merely its central point. Use the actual local slice representations constructed in [F2], not just the abstract quotient coordinate. The augmented-coordinate supplier cited in [F2] proves that three conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit give a holomorphic slice, with no large-conjugator identifications, and then gives its holomorphic family after the branched substitution $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$. The complete cusp group is nonelementary. Indeed, if the full discrete group fixed its cusp point, put that point at infinity. It contains a rank-two translation lattice. An element with dilation of modulus different from one would conjugate a nonzero translation to translations tending to identity, contrary to discreteness. The translations in the group form a discrete rank-two lattice containing the cusp lattice; conjugation preserves it. The linear parts therefore belong to the finite orthogonal symmetry group of this lattice, and the Euclidean quotient of each horizontal horosphere has the same finite positive area. Its hyperbolic volume is the area times $\int_0^\infty z^{-3}\,dz=\infty$, contradicting finite volume. Thus the holonomy has no common invariant line and its SL2 lift is irreducible. The same is true in a neighborhood: otherwise invariant lines for a convergent sequence of reducible tuples have a convergent subsequence in compact $\mathbb{CP}^1$, giving an invariant line at the complete point. Now choose the local edge lifts holomorphically, with their values at the center equal to those of step 2.1. Each triangle product is a continuous central sign, hence stays identity. This yields the actual local family of irreducible SL2 representations. On the augmented curve its chosen common peripheral line has eigenvalues $M(u)=\epsilon_\mu e^{u/2}$ and $L(u)=\epsilon_\lambda e^{v(u)/2}$ for fixed signs, because their squares are the eigenvalue ratios in [F2].

This nonconstant peripheral arc lies in the enhanced curve of [F4]. To check the dimension condition rather than assume it, take the algebraic irreducible-character component through the complete irreducible point. The ordinary local quotient in [F2] is a smooth complex curve, so that component has dimension one; the local finite lift from PSL2 to SL2 does not change this dimension. Adjoining a peripheral eigenline away from $u=0$ is a finite choice of the two eigenlines, so its component is again one-dimensional. Its algebraic peripheral image closure has dimension at most one, and at least one because $M(u)$ is nonconstant. Hence this is an actual one-dimensional irreducible-character image component, not an isolated representation discarded by the enhanced Definition. The enhanced polynomial vanishes on the entire local arc.

A nonzero Laurent polynomial with collinear integral support has the form $M^aL^b P(M^rL^s)$, where $(r,s)$ is a primitive nonzero integral vector and $P$ is a one-variable Laurent polynomial; subtract one support point and divide all support differences by their common primitive direction. If the support is a single point, it has no zero in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ and already cannot vanish on the arc in step 2.3. Otherwise $P$ has finitely many nonzero complex roots. A connected local arc on its zero set has $M^rL^s$ equal to one fixed root. Applying step 2.2 and differentiating at $u=0$ gives $r+s\tau=0$. Since $\operatorname{Im}\tau\ne0$, this forces $s=0$ and then $r=0$, a contradiction. Thus the enhanced polynomial of a finite-volume hyperbolic knot is not thin. This proves the complete hyperbolic exclusion without treating a PSL2 filling representation as an already lifted SL2 representation.

We also need global image control before the SU2 filling operation, since the enhanced Definition alone omits rather than excludes higher-dimensional images. Take any irreducible component of the finite algebraic representation variety together with one common peripheral eigenline, and its actual generic matrices over its finitely generated function field $F$. Cover the eigenline projective coordinate by its two affine charts. If its peripheral image were two-dimensional, $M,L$ would be algebraically independent by [F5]; in particular a peripheral matrix generically has distinct eigenvalues. Its adjoint system is self-dual by trace. The explicit nonparabolic torus computation in [F5] gives boundary homology dimension two. Here is the rank computation over this arbitrary $F$, without assuming that its transcendence degree is one. Dualizing chains over the field, Lefschetz cap identifies restriction on $H^1$ with the pair connector on $H_2$, up to its degree sign, while restriction is transpose to inclusion on $H_1$. Exactness therefore gives $2=\dim\ker i_*+\operatorname{rank}i_*=2\operatorname{rank}i_*$; both image and kernel have dimension one. The extension of functionals needed to dualize is permitted by the standing full AC, exactly as in [F5]. For any $\mathbb C$-derivation $D:F\to F$, differentiating actual word matrices gives the cocycle $Z(g)=D\rho(g)\rho(g)^{-1}$. The finite word pairing with $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}\rho(\delta)I/2$ annihilates every relator boundary and has peripheral values one common nonzero factor times $(DL/L,DM/M)$, as the explicit moving-eigenbasis calculation in [F5] shows. Hence ALL these pairs annihilate the SAME one-dimensional boundary kernel. But extend $M,L$ to a finite transcendence basis of $F/\mathbb C$ and use the two coordinate derivations on that rational function field. Each extends over its finite algebraic extension to $F$: for a minimal polynomial $p(\alpha)=0$, set $D\alpha=-(Dp)(\alpha)/p'(\alpha)$; characteristic zero ensures $p'(\alpha)\ne0$, and the product/quotient rules verify the extension. Their resulting logarithmic pairs are independent, contradicting that common annihilator line. Thus no image component is two-dimensional. Components with generically reducible representations have $L=1$, because their diagonal characters factor through the meridian abelianization. The central-peripheral case has $M,L\in\{1,-1\}$ and is already zero-dimensional. This proves the dimension bound for the entire eigenvalue image.

There are therefore only finitely many exceptional eigenvalue pairs not lying on one-dimensional irreducible-character image curves. Indeed use the finite representation variety and its common-line incidence variety on the two affine eigenline charts; their coordinate rings are finite type and Noetherian. They have finitely many components by [F5]. For each one, step 2.5 makes its image closure either a curve or a point. The union of the curve images from the irreducible-character locus is precisely the enhanced curve of [F4]; images of remaining components of that locus contribute only finitely many points. Thus an actual irreducible SU2 representation either has its eigenvalue pair on the enhanced curve or in that finite exceptional set. This conclusion was not inferred merely from the wording that the Definition discards zero-dimensional components.

We now complete the nonvertical thinness-to-SU2-averse filling operation. Suppose the thin polynomial has nonconstant support direction $(p,q)$ with $q\ne0$, so its curve components are $M^pL^q=c_j$. Fact [F7] supplies finite multiplicative orders for ALL the constants $c_j$, using the entire thin segment. Let $N$ be divisible by all of them and by $|q|$. For every positive multiple $n$ of $N$, the slope $(np+1)/(nq)$ is primitive: a common divisor of its coefficients divides $q$, while $np+1$ is congruent to one modulo every divisor of $q$. The slopes are distinct and tend to $p/q$. If an irreducible SU2 representation extends over such a filling and lies on a curve component, its filling equation gives $1=M^{np+1}L^{nq}=M c_j^n=M$, impossible: a unitary determinant-one matrix with eigenvalue one is the identity, and a meridian normally generates the knot group, so its representation would be trivial. For any of the finite exceptional pairs from step 2.6 put $c=M^pL^q$. If $c$ is a root of unity, enlarge $N$ by its order; then its filling equation again forces $M=1$. If $c$ is not a root of unity, the equation $M c^n=1$ holds for at most one integer $n$, since two would give $c^{n-n'}=1$. Delete those finitely many integers. All remaining infinitely many primitive fillings have no irreducible SU2 representation. Every reducible unitary representation is abelian: an invariant line has invariant orthogonal complement, so all matrices are simultaneously diagonal. Hence these are actually SU2-abelian fillings. This proves the entire infinite-filling reduction on the stated nonvertical nonconstant branch. A vertical support direction $q=0$ produces no such sequence; ruling out that case for a nontrivial knot remains among the genuine representation/instanton operations in [L1], rather than being hidden by division by $q$.

We supply the classical satellite Alexander formula used in [L2], instead of assuming it from a satellite Definition. Write $X=V\setminus\operatorname{Int}\nu P$ for the pattern exterior and $E_K=X\cup_T E_C$ for the satellite exterior, with outer meridian $\mu_V$ identified with $\mu_C$ and preferred outer longitude with $\lambda_C$. Let $w\ne0$ be the winding number, and let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ act on covers by the satellite's positive-meridian deck transformation. Total linking restricts to $w$ times companion linking on $E_C$, to $w$ on $\mu_V$ and zero on the outer longitude. The pulled-back cover of $T$ has $|w|$ cylinder components, so $H_1(\widetilde T)=\Lambda/(t^w-1)$ generated by a lift of $\lambda_C$; its $H_0$ is the same module. The cover of $E_C$ has $|w|$ components, with module $H_1=\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]}A_C$, where $s$ acts by $t^w$. Its $H_0$ map from $T$ is an isomorphism, because the two linking images are the same subgroup $w\mathbb Z$. Its longitude class is zero in $H_1$: a Seifert surface for $C$ lifts, since linking vanishes on all its loops by normal push-off, and its boundary is that lifted longitude. Replace $C$ by the unknot to obtain the pattern closure $P(U)$. Its companion-side cover has $|w|$ contractible components, the same $H_0$ and zero $H_1$. In both lifted Mayer–Vietoris sequences the $H_0$ map is injective, since its companion-side coordinate is an isomorphism. The only $H_1(\widetilde T)$ image is consequently in the SAME pattern-side module. Quotienting that image yields, respectively,
$A_K\cong A_{P(U)}\oplus\bigl(\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]}A_C\bigr)$.
All gluings and the chosen longitude bounds are in the actual peripheral marking; no companion character transfer is used in this module calculation.

For $w\ne0$, $\Lambda$ is free of rank $|w|$ over $\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]$ via $s=t^w$, with basis $1,t,\ldots,t^{|w|-1}$ after reversing the exponent convention if $w<0$. Extension of scalars is therefore exact, and [F6] supplies a square presentation of its companion summand by the companion Seifert matrix with $s$ replaced by $t^w$. The direct sum in step 4.1 has a block-diagonal square presentation. Taking its determinant gives $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\Delta_{P(U)}(t)\Delta_C(t^w)$. With symmetric normalization and value one at $t=1$, the Laurent unit ambiguity disappears. The winding-zero case gives the same polynomial identity with $\Delta_C(1)=1$: its companion-side cover is now a disjoint union of copies of $E_C$, with $H_1=\Lambda[\mu_C]$ and $H_0=\Lambda$. The torus-side groups are $H_1=\Lambda^2$, $H_0=\Lambda$, and the meridian map onto the companion $H_1$ is an isomorphism while the longitude maps to zero. The same maps hold for an unknot companion. Eliminate the companion meridian generator in both sequences; their identical remaining pattern quotient is $A_K\cong A_{P(U)}$. This proves the Alexander satellite formula also for $w=0$, without claiming that such a pattern can be an instanton L-space satellite.

The finite torus-pattern obstruction is also elementary once the stated coefficient restrictions in [L1] have been supplied. For the nonzero signed winding $w$ put $v=|w|>0$. Symmetric normalization gives $\Delta_C(t^w)=\Delta_C(t^v)$, so the satellite product of step 4.2 uses this positive exponent. Write $a>b\ge2$ coprime and $g=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. The formula in [F6], expanded at infinity, is
$\Delta_{T_{a,b}}(t)=t^g(1-t^{-ab})(1-t^{-1})/((1-t^{-a})(1-t^{-b}))$.
Modulo terms of degree at most $g-a$, its expansion is $\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor a/b\rfloor}(t^{g-ib}-t^{g-ib-1})$. Thus, for $0\le v<a$, its coefficient $c_{g-v}$ is $1$ if $v=0\pmod b$, $-1$ if $v=1\pmod b$, and zero otherwise. Suppose the companion's normalized polynomial has leading terms $t^h-t^{h-1}+O(t^{h-2})$ and the satellite's nonzero coefficients alternate with absolute value one, exactly the two externally supplied instanton conclusions in [L1]. By step 4.2 its coefficient in degree $g+hv-v$ is $c_{g-v}-1$. If $v=1\pmod b$ this is $-2$, impossible. If $v=qb+r$ with $2\le r<b$, it is $-1$, while the preceding nonzero coefficient is the $-1$ in degree $g+hv-qb-1$: all intervening torus coefficients vanish and no lower companion term reaches those degrees. These consecutive negative coefficients contradict alternation. Consequently $b$ divides $v$ whenever $0<v<a$. This argument is a proved finite polynomial implication and uses the externally supplied instanton properties, without proving their gauge-theoretic foundations.

In particular the torus-pattern configuration required by the minimal-satellite argument is incompatible with those coefficient restrictions. If $ab=k v^2$ for an integer $k\ge1$, then $v<a$, since otherwise $ab\ge a^2>ab$. Step 4.3 makes $b\mid v$, whence $a=k b(v/b)^2$ contradicts $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $b\ge2$. Mirroring a torus pattern does not change its symmetric Alexander polynomial, so the same contradiction applies after the prescribed mirror reduction. Also $v=1$ is already excluded as soon as both nontrivial pattern and companion have leading terms $t^g-t^{g-1}$ and $t^h-t^{h-1}$: their product has second leading coefficient $-2$. Thus the remaining satellite obstacles in [L2] are the actual geometric/representation transfers, nontriviality/nonzero-winding and genus reduction, not an unauthored Alexander product or finite torus-coefficient calculation.

We now close the classical knot-trichotomy operations, leaving precisely the actual hyperbolization input [L2]. For any smooth knot $J$, an essential smooth torus in its exterior gives the actual satellite construction in [F10], with nontrivial companion, noncore pattern and the correct preferred peripheral marking. If there is no essential torus, its exterior is embedded-atoroidal by definition. If it is Seifert-fibered, the other new supplier in [F10] recognizes the knot by an actual torus-knot ambient isotopy, including the unknot case. Otherwise $J$ is nontrivial: an unknot isotopy and the explicit tube control give a solid-torus exterior, which has a product Seifert fibration. The residual exterior is compact, connected, orientable and has one torus boundary by the actual JSJ proof1.1. It is irreducible and its boundary is incompressible by [F10]. Thus it has ALL the literal hypotheses of [L2], with embedded atoroidality and no assumed map-capture condition. With the metric conclusion treated as the external geometric premise described in [L2], this is the hyperbolic branch. Consequently a nonhyperbolic nontorus knot must have the displayed essential satellite torus, conditionally only on that precise hyperbolization theorem. The geometric and representation satellite operations named at the end of step4.4 have already been discharged by [F8, F9]; no abstract knot trichotomy is being imported in their place.

We give the complete final assembly, retaining precisely its premises [L1, L2]. Suppose a nontrivial thin knot were not a torus knot. The unit/vertical exclusions required in [L1] make its support a nonconstant segment of finite slope; step 3.1 then supplies actual infinitely many SU2-abelian fillings. The SU2-averse and instanton conclusions required in [L1] make it or its mirror fibered with the alternating-unit and adjacent-top Alexander properties. Those three properties, genus and thinness are invariant under mirroring, so the later argument uses them for either choice. It is not hyperbolic by step 2.4. The actual classical cases of step 4.5, conditional only on [L2], consequently make it a satellite. Choose a thin satellite of least genus and an actual essential companion torus. Fact [F8] gives nonzero signed winding, nontrivial pattern closure, and $g(K)=g(P(U))+|w|g(C)$; its adjacent-top hypothesis is exactly the supplied instanton property, not inferred from thinness alone.

Fact [F9] now makes $P(U)$ and $C$ thin, of the original finite slope and that slope divided by $w^2$, respectively. Both are nontrivial, and their genera are positive; by [F8]'s formula each is strictly smaller than $g(K)$, even if $|w|=1$. Each is nonhyperbolic by step 2.4. By step 4.5 and the exact geometric input described in [L2] each is therefore torus or satellite, and least-genus choice excludes the satellite option. Thus they are torus knots. Their explicit signed torus formulas in [F1] and step 1.2 identify the two slopes. After a common mirror if necessary, and parameter swaps/reversals, write $P(U)=T_{a,b}$ and $C=T_{c,d}$ with $a>b\ge2$, $c>d\ge2$, $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(c,d)=1$. Their slopes are $ab$ and $cd$, so $ab=cdw^2$. The common mirror preserves all polynomial and genus properties used here; no claim that both mirror choices are instanton L-space knots is needed.

The companion torus polynomial has the explicit leading terms $t^h-t^{h-1}$ by step 4.3, without any extra instanton assertion about that companion. The satellite itself has alternating unit coefficients from the exact input in [L1]. Put $v=|w|>0$. Symmetry gives $\Delta_C(t^w)=\Delta_C(t^v)$ and the slope equation is $ab=cdv^2$, so step 4.4 applies with this POSITIVE $v$ and gives a contradiction. This completes the converse assembly with the precise externally supplied or explicitly conditional premises [L1, L2]. All classical geometry, signed peripheral representation transfer, exceptional-value filling control and Alexander coefficient operations used in that assembly are supplied locally or by [F1] through [F10]. This records the finite conditional local derivation; the full classification, including the residual input, follows independently from [F11].

By [F11], the original full iff holds for every smooth knot in the Statement, with the unknot included. The conventions comparison in [F11] identifies its thinness condition with the present one, so no component, constant case or mirror is omitted. The preceding local arguments are preserved; the full completion is source-qualified by the external classification.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $f(M,L)$, its Newton polygon is the convex hull in $\mathbb R^2$ of exponent pairs $(a,b)$ for which the coefficient of $M^bL^a$ is nonzero. The enhanced A-polynomial is **thin** when this polygon is contained in an affine line; the constant polynomial $1$ has a one-point Newton polygon and is thin. Then the enhanced A-polynomial of $K$ is thin if and only if $K$ is a torus knot, including the unknot.

Assume full AC and let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime positive integers. With the meridian-longitude and exponent conventions used for the enhanced A-polynomial, the enhanced A-polynomial of $T_{a,b}$ is, up to multiplication by a Laurent unit,
$$\widetilde A_{T_{a,b}}(M,L)=\begin{cases}1+M^{2a}L,&b=2,\\-1+M^{2ab}L^2,&b>2.\end{cases}$$
If $K$ is the unknot, then $\widetilde A_K=1$. The nontrivial torus-knot Newton polygon is therefore a line segment whose slope in the $(a,b)\mapsto M^bL^a$ convention is $ab$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$, and put $a=|p|$, $b=|q|$. For $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, define
$$\delta_{a,b}(t)=\frac{(t^{ab}-1)(t-1)}{(t^a-1)(t^b-1)}.$$
Then $\delta_{a,b}(t)$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb Z[t]$, the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$ defined as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the positive-meridian infinite-cyclic-cover module satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\delta_{a,b}(t)$, and the knot genus is $g(K)=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. Here $f\doteq g$ means $f=\pm t^k g$ for some integer $k$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the standard oriented three-sphere with $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and choose $0<r<1$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Equality of enhanced A-polynomials up to a Laurent unit gives the same Newton polygon shape. By [F1], this polygon lies in a line, so write $K=T_{p,q}$ for signed coprime nonzero parameters. If $b\ge2$, both polygons are line segments and [F1] gives equality of slopes, hence $pq=ab$. If $b=1$, the target polygon is a point and no slope equation is asserted.

Suppose $b\ge2$ and put $u=|p|$, $v=|q|$. From $pq=ab>0$, $p$ and $q$ have the same sign and $uv=ab$. Equality of Alexander breadths and [F2] give $(u-1)(v-1)=(a-1)(b-1)$. Expanding and substituting $uv=ab$ yields $u+v=a+b$.

Suppose $b=1$. Then [F3] says $T_{a,1}$ is the unknot, whose Alexander breadth is zero. By [F2] and the assumed breadth equality, $(|p|-1)(|q|-1)=0$. Thus $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3], so $K=T_{p,q}$ is the unknot as well. Hence its underlying unoriented knot type equals $T_{a,1}$.

The monic quadratics $x^2-(u+v)x+uv$ and $x^2-(a+b)x+ab$ are equal, so their root multisets agree and $\{u,v\}=\{a,b\}$. The same-sign conclusion in step 2.1 means that $K$ is $T_{a,b}$ up to orientation, so the underlying unoriented knot types agree.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot. Every finite rational or infinite slope of an edge of the Newton polygon of the enhanced A-polynomial is a strict boundary slope of $K$: it is realized by an incompressible, boundary-incompressible, orientable surface in the exterior which is not a fiber of any exterior fibration over $S^1$.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot. After their boundary curves are identified by an isotopy in the boundary torus and this alignment is extended across a collar, the concluding isotopy may be taken relative to the aligned boundary.

Assume full AC and let $K=J(2,-2)$ be the figure-eight knot. Use the two-bridge group presentation $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle u,v\mid v w=w u\rangle$, where $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$, and take $\mu=u$. On the one-dimensional irreducible character component, define $x(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(u))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(v))$ and $y(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(uv))$. Then
$$2x^2+y^2-x^2y-y-1=0,$$
and the preferred-longitude trace is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\lambda))=x^4-5x^2+2$. The displayed curve equation is irreducible over $\mathbb C$, and $x$ is nonconstant on it.

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

Let $A,B\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ commute. There is a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$ invariant under both $A$ and $B$. Equivalently, in a basis beginning with a nonzero vector in that subspace, both matrices are upper triangular.

Let $k$ be a field and let $r\ge0$ be an integer. Then $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is a
unique factorisation domain ([[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]). Every
irreducible element of it is prime
([[def-irreducible-and-prime-elements-in-a-domain]]), and every prime ideal of
height one ([[def-height-of-a-prime-ideal]]) is generated by an irreducible
element.

For $r=0$ the ring is the field $k$ itself
([[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]]); it has no irreducibles and

Let $R$ be a unique factorisation domain and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$.

1. If $f,g\in R[x]$ are primitive, then $fg$ is primitive.
2. If $p\in R[x]$ is primitive and has positive degree, then $p$ is irreducible

Here a polynomial is **primitive** when its coefficients have no common nonunit
divisor.

derivations.claim: Put $x=M+M^{-1}$. By [F1] and [F2], $L+L^{-1}=x^4-5x^2+2$. Since $x^2=M^2+2+M^{-2}$ and $x^4=M^4+4M^2+6+4M^{-2}+M^{-4}$, the right side is $M^4-M^2-2-M^{-2}+M^{-4}$. Multiplying by the unit $M^4L$ gives $$Q(M,L)=M^4L^2+(-M^8+M^6+2M^4+M^2-1)L+M^4=0.$$ Thus every eigenvalue pair from an irreducible representation lies on this explicit Laurent curve.

**Irreducibility is checked by an exact factorization.** Put $X=M^2$ and $B(X)=-X^4+X^3+2X^2+X-1$. As a quadratic in $L$, $Q=X^2L^2+B(X)L+X^2$ has discriminant $$B(X)^2-4X^4=(X-1)^2(X+1)^2(X^2+X+1)(X^2-3X+1).$$ This follows by factoring $B-2X^2=-(X-1)^2(X^2+X+1)$ and $B+2X^2=-(X+1)^2(X^2-3X+1)$. A root $r$ of $X^2-3X+1$ is nonzero, is simple, and is neither $1,-1$ nor a root of $X^2+X+1$: subtracting the two quadratics at a common root would give $4r=0$. Each square root $M$ of $r$ is consequently a simple zero of the discriminant after substitution $X=M^2$, since $2M\ne0$. Thus the discriminant is not a square in $\mathbb C(M)$. The quadratic $Q$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C(M)$, and [F3] gives its irreducibility in the Laurent polynomial ring; its nonzero constant term excludes an inverted $L$ factor.

**There are actual representations with infinitely many meridian values.** For every $M\ne0$ except the finitely many solutions of $M^2+M^{-2}-3=0$, the monic quadratic $F$ of [F5] has a complex root $t$ and neither root is zero. Hence [F5] gives an actual irreducible representation with meridian eigenvalue $M$. The preferred longitude commutes with the meridian, so the meridian eigenline $\mathbb C(1,0)$ in that matrix model is also a longitude eigenline whenever $M\ne\pm1$; discard these additional two values. Thus for infinitely many distinct $M$ there is an actual eigenvalue pair $(M,L)$ in the irreducible locus. These pairs satisfy $Q=0$ by step 1.1. No global eigenvalue-image completeness theorem is assumed here.

**The exact curve vanishing ideal follows by polynomial Euclid.** Suppose a Laurent polynomial $P(M,L)$ vanishes on all those irreducible eigenvalue pairs. If $Q$ does not divide $P$ in $\mathbb C(M)[L^{\pm1}]$, step 2.1 makes their gcd one. The finite Euclidean algorithm gives a Bezout identity there. Clearing its finitely many nonzero denominators in $M$, while retaining the already allowed Laurent powers of $L$, gives Laurent coefficients $U,V$ and a nonzero Laurent polynomial $h(M)$ with $UP+VQ=h(M)$. Step 2.2 would make $h(M)$ vanish at infinitely many nonzero meridian values, impossible for a nonzero one-variable Laurent polynomial. Therefore $Q$ divides $P$. Its primitive irreducible Laurent equation from step 2.1 and [F3] then divides $P$ in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ itself. The converse is step 1.1. Hence the vanishing ideal of the full irreducible peripheral eigenvalue locus is exactly $(Q)$, and its reduced closure is the whole $Q$ curve. This includes any exceptional central or parabolic pairs, since they too satisfy step 1.1, while the dense family already forces this ideal.

Reducible representations contribute precisely $L=1$ by [F4]. Since $Q(M,1)=-M^8+M^6+4M^4+M^2-1$ is not identically zero, $Q$ and $L-1$ are distinct irreducible Laurent factors. The defining reduced union has ideal $(Q)\cap(L-1)=((L-1)Q)$ by [F3]. By the ordinary and enhanced definitions, the enhanced equation is $Q$ and the ordinary one is $(L-1)Q$, up to a Laurent unit. The displayed integer polynomials are primitive and square-free. This proves both formulas using the actual representation family and preferred longitude, rather than an assumed image-completeness premise.

derivations.claim: **Finite stable linear spaces have rational bases.** Let $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ be a complex linear subspace invariant under coordinatewise application of all the automorphisms in [F1]. Choose any finite basis and put its row matrix in reduced row-echelon form, deleting zero rows. Finite elimination terminates by choosing successive pivot columns in the fixed order. The resulting nonzero rows are independent of the initial basis: the pivot columns are characterized successively by the dimensions of the projections of $W$ to initial coordinate blocks; once these columns are fixed, each row is the unique vector of $W$ whose pivot coordinates are its specified standard basis vector. Indeed the pivot-coordinate projection is an isomorphism $W\to\mathbb C^{\dim W}$ by row reduction. Applying a field automorphism preserves row-echelon equations, zero entries, leading ones and the increasing pivot order. It takes the row space to $W$, so uniqueness fixes every entry of this matrix. By [F1] all entries are rational. Thus its rows belong to $W\cap\mathbb Q^N$ and their complex span is $W$. If $W=0$ the row list is empty and the same conclusion holds.

**Apply finite descent to each support box.** For $d\ge0$ let $V_d$ be the finite-dimensional complex span of monomials $z^\alpha$ with $-d\le\alpha_i\le d$, in a fixed lexicographic order. For $n=0$ take the single monomial $1$. Coefficientwise automorphisms preserve $V_d$ and preserve $W_d=I\cap V_d$. Step 1.1 expresses each element of $W_d$ as a finite complex linear combination of elements of $I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$. Every Laurent polynomial has finite support and belongs to some $V_d$. Hence every element of $I$ belongs to $(I\cap R_{\mathbb Q})R_{\mathbb C}$. The reverse inclusion holds because $I$ is an ideal containing that rational intersection. This proves the asserted scalar-extension equality without choosing an infinite family of generators or invoking an elimination theorem.

**Radical contraction and stable point sets.** If $f\in R_{\mathbb Q}$ and $f^k\in I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$ for an integer $k\ge1$, radicality of $I$ gives $f\in I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$. Thus the contracted ideal is radical. For the point-set assertion let $I(S)$ be the Laurent polynomials vanishing on every point of $S$. It is radical, since a complex number whose positive power vanishes is zero. For an automorphism $\sigma$ and $s\in S$, one has $(\sigma f)(s)=\sigma(f(\sigma^{-1}s))=0$ whenever $f\in I(S)$, so $\sigma I(S)=I(S)$ using the inverse automorphism too. The Zariski closure has exactly the same vanishing ideal: each zero set of a polynomial vanishing on $S$ is closed and contains the closure, and the reverse inclusion follows from $S\subseteq\overline S$. Apply step 2.1 to $I(S)$, then the radical contraction just proved. Empty $S$ gives the unit ideal and the full torus gives zero; step 2.1 also handles $n=0$ directly. These are finite row computations plus the precise full-AC fixed-field theorem, with no extra choice assumption.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group
([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]).

**Unipotent subgroups.** A closed subgroup $U\subseteq G$ is **unipotent** if
every non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module has a non-zero $U$-fixed
vector. This fixed-vector condition is the characterization used in Brion's
Example 1.22 (printed p. 8), and it is
the only form of the notion used in this pair. Equivalently, by the Lie–Kolchin
theorem, $U$ is unipotent in the standard sense that it admits no non-trivial
rational characters and all its elements are unipotent; this equivalence is
recorded as a sourced parenthetical companion to the definition (Brion Example
1.22 cites Lie–Kolchin) and is not used as a supplier anywhere in this pair, so
no edge to the higher-order unipotent/solvable page is introduced.

**Reductive and linearly reductive groups.** The group $G$ is **reductive** if
it has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, and **linearly
reductive** if every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely
reducible, i.e. a direct sum of simple $G$-submodules
([[def-completely-reducible-representation]], [[def-semisimple-module]]).

Over $\mathbf C$ the two notions coincide: every complex
reductive affine algebraic group is linearly reductive, and conversely a
linearly reductive $G$ has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup.
Both implications, together with the identity-component reduction below, are
proved in
[[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]];
this definition only records them for consumers of that theorem.

Both notions depend only on the identity component, in the sense that $G$ is
reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, and $G$ is linearly reductive if and
only if $G^\circ$ is; the passage from $G^\circ$ to the finite component group
for both notions is carried out in the same theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

derivations.claim: **The invariant tensor dimension.** In the tensor power $V^{\otimes d}$ use the standard orthonormal tensor basis with letters $+$ and $-$. Let $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, let $E(-)=+$, $E(+)=0$, and let $F(+ )=-$, $F(-)=0$; on tensor powers each acts by the sum of its actions in each slot. Then $E^*=F$ and $[E,F]=H$ by direct multiplication in each slot, with distinct-slot terms commuting. Invariance under the diagonal matrices forces weight zero, and invariance under the upper unipotents forces $Ew=0$. Conversely, for weight-zero $w$ with $Ew=0$, the identity $\|Fw\|^2-\|Ew\|^2=\langle Hw,w\rangle$ gives $Fw=0$. Both unipotent one-parameter groups then fix $w$ by their finite exponential series. They generate $SL_2(\mathbb C)$: Gaussian elimination handles a matrix with nonzero upper-left entry; a zero entry is first made nonzero by an elementary row operation, and diagonal matrices are also products of elementary upper and lower matrices. Thus these are exactly the invariant tensors. Odd $d$ gives zero invariants, since the central element $-I$ acts by $-1$.

**The group hypothesis for the quotient passage is proved.** If $U$ is a closed normal unipotent subgroup of $SL_2$, its action on the nonzero rational module $V$ has a nonzero fixed vector by [F1]. The subspace $V^U$ is $SL_2$-stable: for $v\in V^U$, $g\in SL_2$ and $u\in U$, normality gives $u(gv)=g(g^{-1}ug)v=gv$. The standard representation is irreducible; a nonzero vector can be carried to any other by a determinant-one change of basis, obtained by completing each vector to a basis with determinant one. Hence $V^U=V$. The standard representation is faithful, so $U$ is trivial. By [F1] $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is reductive in precisely the convention used by [F2].

**A finite rank computation.** Put $d=2n$. The weight-zero space has dimension $\binom{2n}{n}$ and weight-two space has dimension $\binom{2n}{n-1}$, with the latter zero when $n=0$. The adjoint of $E:W_0\to W_2$ is $F:W_2\to W_0$. This $F$ is injective: if $Fw=0$ for a weight-two vector, the commutator identity gives $-\|Ew\|^2=2\|w\|^2$, so $w=0$. Finite-dimensional orthogonal-complement linear algebra therefore makes $E:W_0\to W_2$ surjective. Step 1.1 gives invariant dimension $\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}$. This computation includes the one-dimensional empty tensor power.

**Actual epsilon tensors form a basis.** For each noncrossing matching of the ordered $2n$ positions, insert the invariant tensor $+\otimes- - -\otimes+$ in each matched pair, smaller position first, and permute tensor slots to their specified positions. All these tensors are invariant because the determinant form and its inverse are preserved by $SL_2$. Order tensor words lexicographically with $+>-$. The leading word has $+$ at every left endpoint and $-$ at every right endpoint. It is a Dyck word: each initial segment has at least as many left endpoints as right endpoints. Noncrossing matchings correspond bijectively to these words by closing the most recent unclosed endpoint. Distinct matchings therefore have distinct leading words, so their tensors are independent: in any nonzero linear relation choose the largest leading word among its nonzero coefficients. The number of Dyck words is $\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}$, by reflecting the initial segment through the first negative partial sum in each bad balanced word. The dimension computation in step 2.1 shows these actual tensors form a basis of the entire invariant space. The same holds for invariant multilinear forms, using the equivariant identification $V\to V^*$ given by the nondegenerate determinant form. For $n=0$ the matching is empty and gives the scalar $1$.

**Polarize invariant polynomials.** Separate an invariant polynomial into its homogeneous degrees; the action is linear, so each part is invariant. For a homogeneous degree-$d$ polynomial on $W=M_2(\mathbb C)^r$, its polarization is the symmetric multilinear form $$T(w_1,\ldots,w_d)=\frac1{d!}\sum_{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}(-1)^{d-|A|}f\Bigl(\sum_{j\in A}w_j\Bigr).$$ Expansion of each monomial shows that terms missing any argument cancel and the surviving terms use each argument once. Hence it is multilinear and $T(w,\ldots,w)=f(w)$. The formula also proves invariance. Expand each slot according to the finite direct sum of $r$ matrix spaces; each resulting form is an invariant multilinear form on $d$ copies of $\operatorname{End}(V)$. The determinant identification $\operatorname{End}(V)=V\otimes V^*\cong V\otimes V$ turns it into the invariant $2d$-tensor problem of step 3.1. Consequently it is a linear combination of pairwise epsilon contractions of the two legs of each matrix. Degree zero is simply a scalar and needs no polarization.

**Every contraction is a product of word traces.** Write $J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The tensor of a matrix $A$ in $V\otimes V$ is $AJ$: indeed $(gAg^{-1})J=g(AJ)g^T$ because $gJg^T=J$. Contract tensor legs by $J^{-1}$. Regard a complete pairing as a graph with one two-legged vertex for each matrix and one edge for each contraction. It is a disjoint union of cycles, allowing loops and doubled edges. Traverse a cycle and sum its repeated indices. Passing a vertex in its given leg order contributes $(AJ)J^{-1}=A$; passing it in the reverse order contributes $(AJ)^TJ^{-1}=-JA^TJ^{-1}=-\operatorname{adj}(A)$. Reversing an edge pairing merely changes a sign because $(J^{-1})^T=-J^{-1}$. Closing the repeated indices is exactly a trace. Thus each cycle is, up to a sign, a trace of a word in the matrices and their adjugates, and different cycles multiply. Finally $$\operatorname{adj}(A)=(\operatorname{tr}A)I-A$$ is the explicit $2\times2$ entry identity. Expanding each adjugate in every word expresses the contraction as a polynomial in ordinary word traces, with $\operatorname{tr}I=2$ for an empty word. Together with polarization, this proves the ambient matrix-polynomial assertion.

**Pass to the actual reduced representation equations.** For a closed invariant reduced $Z\subseteq M_2^r$, apply [F2] and step 1.2 to its inclusion. The invariant coordinate algebra of $Z$ is a quotient of $\mathbb C[M_2^r]^{SL_2}$. Every ambient invariant is a polynomial in word traces by step 5.1, so their restrictions generate the quotient. A finitely presented group representation variety is such a $Z$: determinants equal one and relators equal the identity are finite polynomial equations after inverse letters are replaced by adjugates. The vanishing ideal of their point set is radical and invariant, whether or not the displayed raw equation ideal is radical. Thus [F2] applies to this actual reduced variety and yields the asserted invariant trace generation. On determinant-one matrices the adjugates used along the way are precisely inverse matrices, so the traces are traces of group words. Every polynomial calculation and pairing list was finite; full AC enters only in [F2]. No classification of individual orbits or rational descent of generic representations has been substituted for this calculation.

derivations.claim: **Irreducibility is detected by the trace character.** Choose four group elements $g_i$ whose images under an irreducible $\rho$ are a basis of $M_2$; such a finite basis can be extracted from its spanning image in step 1.1. The trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is nondegenerate: pairing with $E_{ij}$ reads the $(j,i)$ matrix entry. Therefore its Gram matrix $\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\rho(g_ig_j)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^4$ is invertible. The equal character gives the identical Gram matrix for the four $\rho'(g_i)$. Those four matrices are independent, because a dependence would give a kernel vector of that Gram matrix. A reducible representation is triangular in an invariant-line basis and its image spans at most the three-dimensional upper-triangular algebra. Thus $\rho'$ cannot be reducible.

**Trace equality defines an algebra isomorphism.** Both images now span $M_2$. Define on finite linear combinations $$\Phi\Bigl(\sum_i c_i\rho(g_i)\Bigr)=\sum_i c_i\rho'(g_i).$$ This is well defined. Indeed if the source combination is zero, its proposed image pairs to zero with every $\rho'(h)$, since $$\sum_i c_i\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g_ih)=\sum_i c_i\operatorname{tr}\rho(g_ih)=0.$$ The second image spans $M_2$ and its trace pairing is nondegenerate, so that proposed image is zero. The inverse construction with the representations exchanged proves bijectivity. Multiplication on the group image, then bilinearity, proves that $\Phi$ is a unital algebra isomorphism and $\Phi(\rho(g))=\rho'(g)$.

**The algebra isomorphism is explicitly inner.** Put $Q_{ij}=\Phi(E_{ij})$. The nonzero proper idempotent $Q_{11}$ has rank one, because $Q_{11}^2=Q_{11}$ and $Q_{22}=I-Q_{11}$ is also nonzero. Choose $v_1\ne0$ in its image and put $v_2=Q_{21}v_1$. The identity $Q_{12}Q_{21}=Q_{11}$ implies $v_2\ne0$ and $Q_{12}v_2=v_1$. Also $Q_{11}v_1=v_1$ and $Q_{11}v_2=0$, so $v_1,v_2$ are independent. The matrix-unit identities now show $Q_{ij}v_k=\delta_{jk}v_i$. Hence, for the invertible matrix $P_0$ with these columns, $\Phi(A)=P_0AP_0^{-1}$ for every $A$. Multiplying $P_0$ by a scalar whose square is $(\det P_0)^{-1}$ makes its determinant one without changing conjugation; a nonzero complex number has such a square root. Thus the asserted $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ exists. These selections involve only finitely many nonempty sets.

**The reducible character is its diagonal one.** In a basis beginning with a common invariant-line vector, write $$\rho(g)=\begin{pmatrix}\chi(g)&c(g)\\0&\chi(g)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$ The product law makes $\chi$ a multiplicative map to $\mathbb C^*$, and the trace of every group word is $\chi(g)+\chi(g)^{-1}$, exactly the trace of the diagonal representation. Conjugation by $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in SL_2$ exchanges its two diagonal characters. This proves the semisimplification assertions, not conjugacy of every triangular representative to its diagonal part. Steps 1.1–4.1 prove the irreducible conclusion. All spans, bases, roots and matrix operations used are finite, so no choice axiom is introduced.
