citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. For every ideal $J\subseteq R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$. Together with $V(I(X))=X$ for algebraic $X$, these are inverse inclusion-reversing bijections between radical ideals and algebraic sets. Nonempty irreducible algebraic sets correspond precisely to proper prime ideals, and points to maximal ideals. The empty set corresponds to $R$. For $A=R/I(X)$ the same correspondence identifies radical ideals of $A$ with closed subsets of $X$; in particular $I_X(V_X(H))=\sqrt H$.

Assume also Dependent Choice for the cited minimal-prime existence theorem. Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. Every affine algebraic set $X$ has a finite irredundant decomposition into nonempty irreducible closed subsets, unique up to permutation. These are its maximal irreducible closed subsets. The empty set has the empty decomposition.

For a nonempty affine algebraic set $X$, $\dim X=\dim k[X]$, where the right side is Krull dimension. For this comparison only, extend ring dimension to the zero ring by $\dim(0)=-\infty$; then the equality also holds for $X=\varnothing$.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume full AC. Let $n\ge0$, let $R_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$ and $R_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$, and let $I\subseteq R_{\mathbb C}$ be an ideal invariant under coefficientwise application of every field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$. Then $$I=(I\cap R_{\mathbb Q})R_{\mathbb C}.$$ If $I$ is radical, then $I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$ is radical as well. In particular, if $S\subseteq(\mathbb C^*)^n$ is preserved by all such coordinatewise automorphisms, the radical vanishing ideal of its Zariski closure is the scalar extension of a radical ideal over $\mathbb Q$. This includes the empty set, the whole torus and zero variables. No algebraicity or closedness of $S$ is assumed.

derivations.claim: **Exact radical contraction.** Realize $T\times\mathbb C^{m_b}$ as the closed affine set with coordinates $z_i,v_i,u_j$ and equations $z_iv_i=1$. Its coordinate ring is $R[u_1,\ldots,u_{m_b}]$: replace each $z_i^{-1}$ by $v_i$, and reduce any mixed positive powers using $z_iv_i=1$. Thus the relative assertion of [F1] gives $I(X_b)=\sqrt{J_b}$ in exactly this coordinate ring. A Laurent polynomial $f\in R$ vanishes on the projection of $X_b$ exactly when its pullback, the same expression independent of $u$, vanishes on $X_b$. Its ideal is consequently $\sqrt{J_b}\cap R$. Vanishing on a finite union means vanishing on every member, so $I(S)$ is the stated intersection. Moreover $I(S)=I(\overline S)$: each polynomial zero set containing $S$ contains its closure, and $S\subseteq\overline S$ gives the reverse inclusion. This proves the first formula without asserting that a projection is closed. For no charts, $S$ is empty and every polynomial vanishes on it.

**Select actual curve components.** The set $Z$ is a closed subset of the displayed affine model for $T$, so [F2] gives its finite component list $Z_i$. Select precisely the members of dimension one, with dimension as in [F3]. This is a finite union of closed sets, hence closed. A polynomial vanishes on that union exactly when it vanishes on each selected member, giving the second formula directly. Each component ideal is radical, since $f^k$ vanishing at all its points forces $f$ to vanish; their intersection is radical as well. If no component is selected its vanishing ideal is the whole ring. The need for selection is literal: in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$, the closed set $V(L-1)\cup\{(2,2)\}$ has ideal $(L-1)\cap(M-2,L-2)$, whereas its selected curve ideal is $(L-1)$. These differ since $L-1$ has value $1$ at $(2,2)$. The line ideal formula follows by substitution $L=1$ in a Laurent polynomial (multiply by a monomial and divide by $L-1$); the point ideal follows by subtracting its value successively in $M$ and $L$. Thus even radical elimination does not itself discard isolated points.

**Rational descent commutes with selection.** A field automorphism $\sigma$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ induces a bijection of $T$ taking $V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ to $V(\sigma f_1,\ldots,\sigma f_r)$; the same assertion for arbitrary collections of equations makes it a Zariski homeomorphism. If $S$ is stable, its closure $Z$ is stable as well. This homeomorphism permutes the maximal irreducible closed subsets by maximality and preserves their dimensions by bijecting all strict chains of irreducible closed subsets, the convention in [F3]. Therefore it preserves $C$. Apply [F4] separately to the stable point sets $Z$ and $C$ to obtain both asserted radical rational contractions. Finally, rational generators for each $J_b$ make $X_b$ stable by applying $\sigma$ to the defining equations and their inverse implications; projection commutes with $\sigma$, so their union $S$ is stable. All arguments include $n=0$, empty charts, empty zero sets and the whole torus.

derivations.claim: **Only the specified scalar signs can occur.** The element $h$ commutes with $x$ and $y$, since it is a power of each. A nonscalar two-by-two complex matrix either has two distinct eigenvalues or has a repeated eigenvalue and a unique one-dimensional eigenspace. In the first case every commuting matrix preserves each eigenspace; in the second it preserves the kernel of the nonzero nilpotent part, which is that unique line. Thus a nonscalar $\rho(h)$ would provide a line invariant under both generator matrices, contradicting irreducibility. Consequently $\rho(h)=\epsilon I$, and determinant one forces $\epsilon=\pm1$. If $b=2$ and $\epsilon=1$, the equation $Y^2=I$ for $Y=\rho(y)$ makes $Y$ diagonalizable because $(z-1)(z+1)$ has distinct roots. Its determinant one forces its two eigenvalues to be equal, so $Y=I$ or $-I$. An eigenline of $\rho(x)$ would then be invariant under both generators. Hence only $\epsilon=-1$ is possible for $b=2$. In every case $\rho(\lambda)=\epsilon\rho(\mu)^{-ab}$, so every common peripheral eigenvalue pair satisfies $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$, including nonsemisimple meridian matrices.

**Choose noncentral roots with noncentral meridian powers.** Fix a permitted sign. For a positive integer $n\ge2$ choose $\zeta_n=\exp(2\pi i/n)$ when $\epsilon=1$ and $\zeta_n=\exp(\pi i/n)$ when $\epsilon=-1$. The first case is used only for $n\ge3$, since $\epsilon=1$ is permitted only when $a,b>2$. Set $\xi=\zeta_a$ and $\eta=\zeta_b$. They satisfy $\xi^a=\eta^b=\epsilon$ and neither is $\pm1$. Also $\xi^{\beta}\ne\xi^{-\beta}$ and $\eta^{\alpha}\ne\eta^{-\alpha}$. Indeed the Bezout identity gives $\gcd(\beta,a)=\gcd(\alpha,b)=1$. In the positive-sign case equality of the two powers would imply $a\mid2\beta$ or $b\mid2\alpha$, impossible for the relevant integer greater than two. In the negative-sign case the roots have orders $2a,2b$; equality would imply $a\mid\beta$ or $b\mid\alpha$, also impossible. These explicit roots require no choice family.

**An actual irreducible matrix family.** Put $s=\eta+\eta^{-1}$ and, for $v\in\mathbb C$, define $$X=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&0\\0&\xi^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y_v=\begin{pmatrix}v&1\\v(s-v)-1&s-v\end{pmatrix}.$$ The second matrix has determinant one and trace $s$, hence distinct eigenvalues $\eta,\eta^{-1}$. Therefore $X^a=Y_v^b=\epsilon I$, and these are actual representations of the displayed presentation for every $v$. Since $X$ has distinct eigenvalues, a common invariant line must be one of its coordinate lines. The upper-right entry of $Y_v$ is $1$, so the second coordinate line is never invariant. The first is invariant exactly when $v(s-v)-1=0$, whose two roots are $\eta,\eta^{-1}$. Thus the representation is irreducible for every $v$ other than these two values.

**The meridian trace varies with a nonzero linear coefficient.** Polynomial division modulo $(z-\eta)(z-\eta^{-1})$ gives $Y_v^\alpha=cY_v+dI$ for constants $c,d$ independent of $v$, including negative $\alpha$ because both eigenvalues are nonzero. Explicitly $c=(\eta^\alpha-\eta^{-\alpha})/(\eta-\eta^{-1})\ne0$ and $d=\eta^\alpha-c\eta$. With $r=\xi^\beta$, one obtains $$\operatorname{tr}(Y_v^\alpha X^\beta)=c(r-r^{-1})v+cr^{-1}s+d(r+r^{-1}).$$ The coefficient is nonzero by step 1.2. For each $M\ne0$ there is consequently exactly one $v$ giving meridian trace $M+M^{-1}$. The two forbidden $v$ values of step 2.1 exclude at most four meridian values, since each equation $M+M^{-1}=q$ is a quadratic after multiplication by $M$. Discard also $M=\pm1$. For every remaining $M$ the meridian has distinct eigenvalues $M,M^{-1}$, so an eigenline with eigenvalue $M$ exists and the longitude, being $\epsilon\mu^{-ab}$, acts there by $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$. This gives the claimed cofinite graph family for each permitted sign.

**Exact ideals, including all exceptional representations.** Evaluation $L\mapsto\epsilon M^{-ab}$ defines a surjection $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]\to\mathbb C[M^{\pm1}]$. Its kernel is $(LM^{ab}-\epsilon)$: multiplying by a monomial reduces any expression to a polynomial in $L$, and division by the monic $L-\epsilon M^{-ab}$ over $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1}]$ leaves exactly its evaluated constant remainder. A Laurent polynomial vanishing on the cofinite graph family of step 3.1 therefore has zero evaluated remainder, since a nonzero one-variable Laurent polynomial has only finitely many nonzero roots. Its ideal is precisely this graph ideal. Step 1.1 puts every irreducible eigenvalue pair, including all exceptional meridian values, in the permitted graphs, and step 3.1 supplies a dense family in each. The ideal of the entire locus and of its closure is consequently the intersection of these graph ideals. For $b=2$ the single sign gives $(LM^{2a}+1)$. For $b>2$ put $q=LM^{ab}$; the two ideals $(q-1)$ and $(q+1)$ are comaximal since their difference is $2$, an invertible scalar. Their intersection equals their product: writing $1=A+B$ with $A$ in one and $B$ in the other expresses an element of the intersection as a sum of two product elements. Thus their intersection is $(q^2-1)=(M^{2ab}L^2-1)$. Each graph ideal is prime because its quotient is the Laurent domain just displayed; their intersection is radical. This proves the exact reduced closure assertions by finite algebra with no assumption about completeness of an unspecified image.

Apply [F1] also to $A+B$ and subtract the identities for $A,B$. The entrywise determinant polarization is $\det(A+B)-\det A-\det B=ab-c$. Hence $$AB+BA=aB+bA+(c-ab)I,$$ an identity valid without any genericity or independence of the four matrices.

The span of $I,A,B,AB$ over $\mathbb Z[a,b,c]$ is stable under right multiplication by $A$ and $B$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

There are the following explicit valid finite planar codes, with the standard right/up orientation of the plane and positive based meridians using compatible common upper-collar access paths.

The counterclockwise square with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ is a crossing-free unknot code. It has one under-arc and gives $\pi_1(S^3\setminus U)=\langle x\mid\ \rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with $x$ the positive meridian.

An oriented figure-eight code has crossings $C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4$. The letters $O,U$ mean over and under, and $i,o$ mean incoming and outgoing. Its integer plane-drawing certificate is

| $r$ | $C_r$ | $rOi$ | $rOo$ | $rUi$ | $rUo$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $(-423,0)$ | $(-627,102)$ | $(-363,-30)$ | $(-363,30)$ | $(-627,-102)$ |
| $2$ | $(0,-9)$ | $(-33,-6)$ | $(99,-18)$ | $(-99,-18)$ | $(33,-6)$ |
| $3$ | $(0,9)$ | $(33,6)$ | $(-99,18)$ | $(99,18)$ | $(-33,6)$ |
| $4$ | $(423,0)$ | $(627,-102)$ | $(363,30)$ | $(363,-30)$ | $(627,102)$ |

The complete cyclic visit list is $$1O,\ 2U,\ 3O,\ 1U,\ 4O,\ 3U,\ 2O,\ 4U.$$ For every successive pair $rB,sD$ in this list, including the last-to-first pair, use the three straight segments of the route $C_r\to rBo\to sDi\to C_s$. At each crossing pair $rOi$ with $rOo$, and $rUi$ with $rUo$; the first pair is over. Smooth the degree-two bends in disjoint small disks. The cyclic orders at crossings are the counterclockwise lists $(rOo,rUi,rOi,rUo)$ for $r=1,4$ and $(rOo,rUo,rOi,rUi)$ for $r=2,3$.

Label the under-arcs $x_1:U4\to U2$, $x_2:U2\to U1$, $x_3:U1\to U3$, $x_4:U3\to U4$. In each oriented over-branch chart, let $L$ denote its left under-side (target of the positive in-plane normal), and $R$ its right under-side (source). The exact crossing table is

| crossing | over | $L$ (target) | $R$ (source) | under traversal | $\operatorname{sign}\det(\text{over},\text{under})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $R_1$ | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $x_3$ | target to source | $-1$ |
| $R_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_2$ | $x_1$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_3$ | $x_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_3$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_4$ | $x_3$ | $x_4$ | $x_1$ | target to source | $-1$ |

Thus its actual positive-meridian presentation is $$\pi_1(S^3\setminus 4_1)=\langle x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\mid x_1x_2=x_3x_1,\ x_1x_4=x_4x_2,\ x_3x_2=x_2x_4,\ x_3x_4=x_1x_3\rangle.$$ The last relation follows from the first three. Starting on $x_1$, the underpasses occur at $R_2,R_1,R_3,R_4$, and the self-writhe is zero. All drawing data, validations and algebra in this statement are finite and use no choice axiom.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

derivations.claim: In [F1] eliminate $x_3$ using $R_1$ to get $X_3=uvu^{-1}$, then eliminate $x_4$ using $R_3$ to get $X_4=v^{-1}X_3v=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v$. These are eliminations of explicitly defined generators, reversible by substitution, so impose exactly the remaining relation $R_2$; $R_4$ adds none by [F1]. With $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$ the expression is $X_4=w^{-1}v$. Hence $R_2$ reads $uw^{-1}v=w^{-1}v^2$, which after right cancellation of $v$ is $uw^{-1}=w^{-1}v$, equivalently $vw=wu$. This proves the asserted presentation with the original positive meridian $u=x_1$.

Start the oriented traversal at $x_1$. The four successive underpasses in [F1] give the table $$(R_2,x_4,+1),\quad(R_1,x_1,-1),\quad(R_3,x_2,+1),\quad(R_4,x_3,-1),$$ listing crossing, over-meridian and source/target exponent. Indeed $R_2,R_3$ go from the lower source side to the upper target side in those actual coordinate charts, while $R_1,R_4$ go from the upper target side to the lower source side. The determinants of their ordered over/under tangents have these same signs: each over-tangent points right and the under-tangent points respectively upwards or downwards. Thus the self-writhe is $1-1+1-1=0$. This checks both the traversal order and the sign instead of deriving a longitude solely from homological exponent zero.

By [F2], the based blackboard parallel for that actual code is $x_4x_1^{-1}x_2x_3^{-1}$. The self-writhe correction in step 1.2 is zero, so this very word is the preferred longitude. Substitution from step 1.1 gives $X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}$. The positive component traversal has degree one in its peripheral tube by [F2], and the zero-writhe correction gives zero self-linking; this is the actual preferred peripheral representative with the chosen initial access path. Evaluating it in any representation proves the trace assertion. No other longitude convention or external two-bridge peripheral formula is assumed.

derivations.claim: **Find a noncentral semisimple word and a word meeting both eigenspaces.** Some group matrix has trace different from $2,-2$. Otherwise, if all matrices were scalar the representation would be reducible; choose a nonscalar $D=\epsilon I+N$ with $\epsilon=\pm1$, $N\ne0$ and $N^2=0$ by [F1]. For every group matrix $C$ and integer $m\ge0$, $$\operatorname{tr}(D^mC)=\epsilon^m\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C+m\epsilon^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(NC)\bigr).$$ All these traces belong to $\{2,-2\}$ by the supposition. In characteristic zero a nonconstant affine function on the nonnegative integers takes infinitely many values, so $\operatorname{tr}(NC)=0$ for every $C$. In a basis over $F$ with $N=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ this forces the lower-left entry of every $C$ to be zero. Its first coordinate line would be invariant, a contradiction. Thus choose a word $A$ with trace different from $\pm2$, and adjoin one root $\xi$ of its characteristic polynomial. Its two distinct eigenvalues are $\xi,\xi^{-1}$, so it is diagonalizable already over $F(\xi)$. In that eigenbasis some group word $B$ has both off-diagonal entries nonzero. Indeed the elements preserving the first and second eigenlines form two proper subgroups of $\Gamma$ by absolute irreducibility. A group cannot be the union of two proper subgroups: for elements in their respective differences, their product belongs to neither. Choose $B$ outside that union. These are finitely many existential selections, not an infinite choice principle.

**Normalize and recover every generator by trace equations.** In the chosen $A$ eigenbasis write $B_{12}=u
e0$ and conjugate by $\operatorname{diag}(u^{-1},1)$ to make this entry one. The lower-left entry becomes the nonzero product $q=B_{12}B_{21}$. Put $a=\operatorname{tr}A$, $b=\operatorname{tr}B$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. In the normalized basis $$A= egin{pmatrix}\xi&0\0&\xi^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad B= egin{pmatrix}d_1&1\q&d_2\end{pmatrix},\quad d_1= rac{c-\xi^{-1}b}{\xi-\xi^{-1}},\quad d_2=b-d_1,\quad q=d_1d_2-1
e0.$$ All these entries lie in $K'=K(\xi)$. For each generator $C$ put $e=\operatorname{tr}C$, $f=\operatorname{tr}(AC)$, $g=\operatorname{tr}(BC)$ and $h=\operatorname{tr}(ABC)$, which belong to $K$ by its definition. Its diagonal entries are $$c_{11}= rac{f-\xi^{-1}e}{\xi-\xi^{-1}},\qquad c_{22}=e-c_{11}.$$ Its off-diagonal entries are uniquely solved from $$c_{21}+q c_{12}=g-d_1c_{11}-d_2c_{22},\qquad \xi c_{21}+\xi^{-1}q c_{12}=h-\xi d_1c_{11}-\xi^{-1}d_2c_{22}.$$ The determinant of this two-by-two linear system is $q(\xi^{-1}-\xi)
e0$. Thus every normalized generator matrix has entries in $K'$. These are the actual conjugated original matrices in $F(\xi)$, not merely formal matrices with the correct traces: the normalization was performed first and the displayed linear equations uniquely recover their entries. Therefore their determinant-one equations and every group relation hold in $K'$, by its injection into $F(\xi)$. The conjugated representation is an actual model over $K'$, with no new relator-existence assumption.

**The quadratic swap is explicit conjugation.** If $K'=K$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise its automorphism $\tau$ exchanges $\xi$ and $\xi^{-1}$ and fixes every word trace. The formulas of step 2.1 give $\tau(d_1)=d_2$, $\tau(q)=q$. Put $$P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&q^{-1}\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Direct multiplication gives $PAP^{-1}=\tau A$ and $PBP^{-1}=\tau B$. For each generator $C$, both $PCP^{-1}$ and $\tau C$ have traces $e,f,g,h$ when paired respectively with $I,\tau A,\tau B,(\tau A)(\tau B)$: conjugation preserves trace, and $\tau$ fixes the four word traces. The diagonal/off-diagonal recovery in step 2.1 applies to this swapped pair as well; its determinant is still nonzero. Uniqueness therefore gives $PCP^{-1}=\tau C$ for every generator, hence for all group words. This proves simultaneous conjugacy over $K'$ itself, without an appeal to pointwise complex-character classification.

**Projective descent for compatible invariant constructions.** Under the hypotheses on $z$, applying $\tau$ to its construction yields the point constructed from $\tau\rho$, while conjugation invariance and step 3.1 identify that point with $z$. Hence $\tau z=z$. Choose one nonzero homogeneous coordinate $z_j$ and normalize it to $1$. Equality of projective points implies that each ratio $z_i/z_j$ is fixed by $\tau$. Every element of the quadratic field has the unique form $u+v\xi$ with $u,v\in K$; being fixed gives $v(\xi-\xi^{-1})=0$, so $v=0$. Thus every normalized coordinate lies in $K$, proving that $z$ is a $K$-point. In the trivial-extension case this is immediate. The argument uses only finite matrix and field operations; it neither asserts that an arbitrary merely pointwise invariant assignment is rational nor supplies any analytic or chain-complex prerequisite for constructing $z$.

Each operation has an explicit inverse and removes one row and column from the remaining problem. It ends after at most the smaller matrix size, with a block identity and a zero rectangle. This proves that its number of pivots is the rank, since invertible operations preserve the column-span dimension and $\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)$ has rank $r$; the same normal form also gives row-span dimension $r$; no real-only rank-minor theorem is invoked. Apply this to $C$, recording its changes of bases in $F^n$ and $F^t$. Its kernel has basis the last $n-\gamma$ domain coordinates. The identity $CB=0$ places every column of the transformed $B$ in those coordinates. Apply the same algorithm to this $(n-\gamma)$-row matrix, using only row operations within $\ker C$ and column operations on $F^s$. Its first $\beta$ coordinates are now the image of $B$, and its remaining $h=n-\gamma-\beta$ coordinates represent the quotient homology. Thus the entire chain pair has a split block form over $F$, not just separately computed nullities.

Ignore its next $ eta$ boundary coordinates and call the remaining $h	imes2$ matrix $V$. The hypothesis on $(B\mid U)$ says exactly that $V$ has rank one: the image of $B$ already fills its own $ eta$ coordinates, while appending $U$ adds the dimension of its quotient image. e0$, use $a$ as the pivot; if $a=0$, then $b
e0$, and use $b$ as the pivot. Each other row is a multiple of $(a,b)$, since otherwise two rows would be independent and the matrix would have rank at least two. Compute each multiple using its first coordinate divided by $a$ when $a
e0$, or its second coordinate divided by $b$ when $a=0$, and subtract that multiple of the pivot row. This makes every other row zero using only the chosen nonzero pivot. Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

derivations.claim: **The fixed line and a rational complementary plane.** The direct $2\times2$ determinant identity gives $M^2-tM+I=0$, and therefore $v^2=(\Delta/4)I$, $\operatorname{tr}v=0$, and $\operatorname{tr}(v^2)=\Delta/2\ne0$. In particular $v\ne0$. The map $\pi:V\to Fv$ defined by $\pi(X)=2\operatorname{tr}(vX)v/\Delta$ is a projection: $\pi(v)=v$, its image is $Fv$ and its kernel is $W$. Thus $V=Fv\oplus W$. Commutation of $L,M$ implies $P(v)=Q(v)=v$. For either $A=L$ or $A=M$, the direct identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(vAXA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}vAX)=\operatorname{tr}(vX)$. Hence $P,Q$ preserve $W$ and commute with $\pi$.

**An actual inverse on the complementary plane.** On $W$ the inverse of $Q-I$ is the explicit operator $R=(Q+(3-t^2)I)/\Delta$. To check this without a splitting-field assumption, the polynomial $z^2-tz+1$ either has a root in $F$ or is irreducible, in which case its quotient gives a quadratic extension. In that field its two distinct roots are $r,r^{-1}$, and a change of basis diagonalizes $M$, since the two kernels of $M-rI$ and $M-r^{-1}I$ are distinct one-dimensional subspaces. In these coordinates $v=\operatorname{diag}((r-r^{-1})/2,-(r-r^{-1})/2)$, $W$ is exactly the off-diagonal plane, and $Q$ has eigenvalues $r^2,r^{-2}$ on it. Consequently $Q^2-(t^2-2)Q+I=0$ on $W$, and multiplication gives $(Q-I)(Q+(3-t^2)I)=\Delta I$ there. This identity descends to $F$, because scalar extension of a finite matrix over a field is injective. The two factors commute, so $R$ is a two-sided inverse. It commutes with $P$ because $P$ commutes with $Q$. This finite calculation uses no chosen eigenvectors in the final formulas.

**The actual torus chain complex.** Use one vertex, the two oriented edges and the square whose attaching path is $\lambda\mu\lambda^{-1}\mu^{-1}$. Lift its lower left corner and transport a coefficient from that corner along its four sides. The bottom and oppositely oriented top edges give coefficients $z$ and $-Qz$ in the $\lambda$ coordinate; the right and oppositely oriented left edges give $Pz$ and $-z$ in the $\mu$ coordinate. Thus the square boundary is $((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$. An edge with monodromy $S$ has boundary $(S-I)$ on its coefficient, which gives $d_1$ as stated. The two composites cancel because $PQ=QP$. This is the supplied-lift cellular model in [F1], so it computes the actual intrinsic homology, rather than an independently assumed complex. The direct-sum decomposition of step1.1 splits this entire complex into its $Fv$ and $W$ parts.

**A chain contraction, including both ends of the complex.** On the $W$ part define $h_0:W\to W\oplus W$ by $h_0(z)=(0,Rz)$ and $h_1:W\oplus W\to W$ by $h_1(x,y)=-Rx$, and put all other homotopy maps zero. Their cycles are precisely the vertex, the two supplied oriented edges, and the supplied oriented square with coefficient $v$. This proves the stated basis and not merely a dimension count.

For simultaneous conjugation by an invertible matrix $A$, the map $X\mapsto AXA^{-1}$ sends $v$ to the new $v$, intertwines $P,Q$, and preserves all traces in $\pi$; it therefore carries the splitting and contraction to the displayed new ones and takes each named peripheral cycle to its corresponding cycle. A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

derivations.claim: **Construct comparison maps in just three degrees.** Lift $\epsilon_C:C_0\to S$ across the surjection $\epsilon_D$ using projectivity of $C_0$, obtaining $f_0:C_0\to D_0$. The image of $f_0d_1$ lies in $\ker\epsilon_D=\operatorname{im}\delta_1$, because $\epsilon_Df_0d_1=\epsilon_Cd_1=0$. Regard $\delta_1:D_1\to\ker\epsilon_D$ as a surjection, and use projectivity of $C_1$ to lift this map to $f_1:C_1\to D_1$ with $\delta_1f_1=f_0d_1$. Now $\delta_1f_1d_2=f_0d_1d_2=0$, so $f_1d_2$ maps into $\ker\delta_1=\operatorname{im}\delta_2$. Lift it across $D_2\to\ker\delta_1$ by projectivity of $C_2$, obtaining $f_2$ with $\delta_2f_2=f_1d_2$. This gives all required chain and augmentation identities. Reversing $C,D$ produces a map $g$ in exactly the same finite way. No exactness in degree2 was used.

**Uniqueness up to the homotopy needed in degree one.** More generally let $f,f':C\to D$ be any two comparison maps lifting the same $1_S$, and put $a_i=f_i-f'_i$. Since $\epsilon_Da_0=0$, projectivity of $C_0$ and exactness at $D_0$ give $h_0:C_0\to D_1$ with $\delta_1h_0=a_0$. The map $a_1-h_0d_1:C_1\to D_1$ has zero composite with $\delta_1$, because $\delta_1a_1=a_0d_1$. By exactness at $D_1$ and projectivity of $C_1$, it therefore lifts to $h_1:C_1\to D_2$ with $\delta_2h_1=a_1-h_0d_1$. Thus $a_0=\delta_1h_0$ and $a_1=\delta_2h_1+h_0d_1$. No further homotopy degree is needed for first homology. This construction applies in particular to the two comparisons $gf$ and $1_C$, and also to $fg$ and $1_D$.

**Tensor the actual identities, without a flatness assumption.** For each left-linear map $u$ used above, define $1\otimes u$ on elementary tensors by $n\otimes c\mapsto n\otimes u(c)$. It respects the balanced relation since $u(rc)=ru(c)$, and it respects the additive relations in [F2]. Consequently these induced maps respect sums, differences, compositions and every chain identity above. If $z\in N\otimes_R C_1$ satisfies $(1\otimes d_1)z=0$, the second identity of step2.1 becomes $((1\otimes f_1)-(1\otimes f'_1))z=(1\otimes\delta_2)(1\otimes h_1)z$, an actual boundary. Chain maps preserve cycles and boundaries, so this proves equality of their induced first-homology maps. Apply it to $gf,1_C$ and $fg,1_D$ to show that the induced maps of $f$ and $g$ are mutually inverse. This uses preserved homotopy identities, not preserved exactness of the tensored augmented complexes. In particular no flatness of $N$ has entered.

**Compatibility, finite choice use and limits.** A composite of augmentation-preserving comparisons is again such a comparison, so the uniqueness in step3.1 identifies its first-homology map with the unique comparison to the third complex. For a homomorphism $q:N\to N'$ of right modules, the tensor maps $q\otimes1$ commute with all $1\otimes f_i$ on each elementary tensor and hence on finite sums; this proves naturality. The same uniqueness shows that a separately supplied geometric or algebraic comparison induces exactly this isomorphism. Each lift in steps1.1–2.1 is supplied by the projectivity of its particular domain, and the proof takes only finitely many successive witnesses, including the reverse map and the two finite homotopies. No choice of lifts in all degrees, all objects or all coefficient modules is required: independence specifies a unique resulting map for each $N$. Zero modules, zero differentials compatible with the exactness assumptions, and the zero coefficient module obey the same equations. The proof neither constructs a topological spine nor assumes that arbitrary coefficient tensoring preserves exactness. This proves all the stated assertions with the prescribed left/right sides over an arbitrary ring.

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
Every nonempty path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space has a universal covering space.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Let $X$ be a nonempty connected CW complex with basepoint $x$, let
$p:\widetilde X\to X$ be a universal cover
([[def-universal-covering-space]], [[thm-universal-cover-existence]]), put
$\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Identify $\pi$
with the deck group by the no-reversal isomorphism of
[[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]]. Write
$g c$ for the induced **left** deck action on a singular or cellular chain.

The **right group-ring action** on universal-cover chains is
$$c\cdot g:=g^{-1}c\qquad(g\in\pi),$$
extended additively and $R$-linearly to [[def-group-ring|$R[\pi]$]]. It is a
right action because
$$(c\cdot g)\cdot h=h^{-1}(g^{-1}c)=(gh)^{-1}c=c\cdot(gh),\qquad c\cdot1=c.$$
Here the multiplication $[g][h]=[gh]$ and the unit $[1]$ are those constructed
in [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]; bilinearity extends the
displayed group action uniquely to all finite formal sums in $R[\pi]$.
Every deck map is cellular for the lifted CW structure and commutes with the
singular and cellular boundaries. Hence
$$\partial(c\cdot g)=(\partial c)\cdot g,$$
and $C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)$ and
$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)$ are chain complexes of right
$R[\pi]$-modules.

Choosing one lift and one orientation of every cell of $X$ makes each cellular
chain group a free right $R[\pi]$-module on those lifted oriented cells. This
is only a basis choice, not part of the chain complex. Empty chain degrees and
the zero ring give zero modules. The inversion in the definition is forced by
the library's first-loop-first deck convention; omitting it would reverse the
balanced tensor formulas below.

For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base $B$, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to $\pi_1(B,b_0)$. With the library's traversal-order path product the monodromy action is a right action, and the assignment carrying a loop class to the deck transformation that moves the chosen point of the fibre to the corresponding lifted endpoint is itself an isomorphism; no path reversal is inserted.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every free module is projective. More precisely, if $F$ has basis $(e_x)_{x\in X}$, a lift of a map $F\to M$ through a surjection $E\to M$ is obtained by choosing one preimage of each basis value. For finite $X$, finite choice suffices and no form of AC is needed; for $X=\varnothing$, the lift is the unique map from $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be any unital ring, let $S$ be a left $R$-module, and let
$$C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_C}S\longrightarrow0,\qquad D_2\xrightarrow{\delta_2}D_1\xrightarrow{\delta_1}D_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_D}S\longrightarrow0$$
be augmented complexes of left $R$-modules, exact at $C_1,C_0,S$ and at $D_1,D_0,S$. Suppose each of the six modules $C_i,D_i$, $0\le i\le2$, is projective. No exactness at $C_2,D_2$ or further degrees is required. There are augmentation-preserving chain maps through degree $2$ between these complexes lifting $1_S$. For every right $R$-module $N$, any such comparison induces the same isomorphism of abelian groups
$$H_1(N\otimes_R C_\bullet)\ \cong\ H_1(N\otimes_R D_\bullet).$$
These isomorphisms are inverse under reversing the complexes, compose for a third such complex, and are natural in homomorphisms of right coefficient modules. In particular a supplied augmentation-preserving chain map through degree $2$ induces this isomorphism; its construction need not be the one chosen in the proof. Tensoring is not assumed exact, and $N$ need not be flat. This is a comparison of supplied algebraic complexes, not an assertion that a presentation complex is a deformation retract or a homotopy-equivalent spine of another space.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$.

The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is
$$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$
Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is
$$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$
and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$.

The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product
$$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$
so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$
Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$.

For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$

For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by
$$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$
Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule
$$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$
not a module-Hom between one right and one left module.

The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term.

The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied.

The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

Let $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ be a map of pairs.

1. A coefficient morphism $\eta:\mathcal L\to f^*\mathcal K$ induces
   $$f_*:H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\longrightarrow H_n(Y,B;\mathcal K).$$
2. A coefficient morphism $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ induces
   $$f^*:H^n(Y,B;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$

At a fixed space, both theories are covariant in coefficient morphisms. These maps preserve identities and composition. If $H:f_0\simeq f_1$ is a homotopy of pair maps, transport along $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ gives $\tau_H:f_0^*\mathcal K\to f_1^*\mathcal K$; the homology maps agree when $\eta_1=\tau_H\eta_0$, and the cohomology maps agree when $\theta_0=\theta_1\tau_H$.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic different from $2$, and let $L,M\in SL_2(F)$ commute. Write $t=\operatorname{tr}M$ and suppose $\Delta=t^2-4\ne0$. Give the torus $T^2$ an ordered pair of based oriented generating loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, and give its adjoint local system intrinsic monodromies $P=\operatorname{Ad}L$ and $Q=\operatorname{Ad}M$ on $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(F)$. Here monodromy acts on column coefficient vectors on the left. Set
$$v=M-\frac t2 I,\qquad W=\{X\in V:\operatorname{tr}(vX)=0\}.$$
Then $V=Fv\oplus W$, both summands are preserved by $P,Q$, and $P,Q$ are the identity on $Fv$. There is an explicit split chain model
$$0\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow{d_2}V\oplus V\xrightarrow{d_1}V\longrightarrow0,$$
where $d_2z=((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$ and $d_1(x,y)=(P-I)x+(Q-I)y$, in the ordered edge coordinates $(\lambda,\mu)$. Its $W$ subcomplex is contractible, so
$$H_0(T^2;V)=F[v],\qquad H_1(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes\lambda]\oplus F[v\otimes\mu],\qquad H_2(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes[T^2]].$$
In particular the two displayed peripheral classes are an actual basis, without imposing any norm-one normalization on $v$. The splitting, contraction and classes commute with field extensions and simultaneous conjugation of $L,M$. All their matrix entries are rational expressions in the entries of $L,M$, with denominators powers of $2$ and $\Delta$. This assertion concerns boundary-torus homology only: it makes no claim about the rank of its inclusion into the homology of a knot exterior.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$

derivations.claim: **Construct the actual presentation map.** Begin with the generator circles and attach the finitely many relator disks. The circle wedge has the free fundamental group in [F1]. For one disk attachment, the old complex together with the outer region $r>1/3$ in the attached disk is an open set deforming to the old complex; the inner region $r<2/3$ is an open contractible disk. Their overlap is an annulus, and its generator maps to the attaching word in the old complex. These are open sets also for a noninjective attaching map, as can be checked on the old complex and the disk before taking the adjunction quotient. Van Kampen therefore quotients the old group by the normal closure of that word. Finite iteration proves $\pi_1(P,p)=\langle x_j\mid r_i\rangle$ with the stated generators. Send the generator circles to the chosen loops in $Y$. Each relator is trivial in $\pi_1(Y,y)$ by the given presentation isomorphism, so its based nullhomotopy descends from the cone on the circle to a filling disk. Choose these finitely many fillings and glue along their attaching circles; the quotient topology gives a continuous map $f:P\to Y$. It induces exactly the prescribed isomorphism. No approximation or CW structure on the target is needed.

**Verify the actual augmented cover complexes.** Put $R=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ and identify the two deck groups by $f_*$. Choose pointed universal covers by [F2]. Use cellular integral chains $C_*(\widetilde P)$ for the presentation cover and singular integral chains $D_*=S_*(\widetilde Y;\mathbb Z)$ for the target cover. Both covers are path-connected and simply connected. Their singular integral $H_0$ is $\mathbb Z$: differences of points bound paths and the sum-of-coefficients augmentation induces this isomorphism. Their singular integral $H_1$ is zero by Hurewicz [F3]. For $\widetilde P$, ordinary cellular comparison in [F3] gives the same two groups. Thus both augmented complexes are exact in degrees1/0 and at the common trivial right module $\mathbb Z$. The right action is $c\cdot g=T_{g^{-1}}c$, and commutes with boundaries. For the cellular domain a lift of each of its finitely many cells is a free right $R$ basis. For the singular target, every singular simplex downstairs has a lift after a lift of its first vertex is prescribed, since its domain is a simply connected simplex; two lifts differ by exactly one deck transformation. The deck action on any lifted simplex is free, since a deck transformation fixing that simplex fixes one of its image points. Consequently one lifted simplex for each downstairs simplex is a free right $R$ basis of $D_k$. AC supplies these simultaneous choices, and projectivity follows from [F3]. This proves the needed exactness and projectivity without a CW target, a UCT calculation or asphericity.

**Identify the target singular tensor complex without a CW hypothesis.** Write $p_Y:\widetilde Y\to Y$ and fix the lifted basepoint $\widetilde y$. For a lifted singular simplex $\widetilde\sigma$, choose a path $\widetilde\beta$ from $\widetilde y$ to its first vertex and put $\beta=p_Y\widetilde\beta$. Define $$\Phi(\widetilde\sigma\otimes a)=(T_\beta a)\,(p_Y\widetilde\sigma)$$ in the intrinsic singular complex of [F5]. Two choices of $\widetilde\beta$ are homotopic relative endpoints in the simply connected cover, so their projected transports agree. Under the no-reversal deck convention, a path to $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g=T_{g^{-1}}\widetilde\sigma$ represents $g^{-1}$ followed by $\beta$. Its transport is $T_\beta T_{g^{-1}}$, and $T_{g^{-1}}a=ga$ by the supplied coefficient convention. Hence $\Phi((\widetilde\sigma\cdot g)\otimes a)=\Phi(\widetilde\sigma\otimes ga)$, exactly the balanced relation. For the zeroth face, the path to its first vertex is $\widetilde\beta$ followed by the lifted edge from vertex0 to vertex1. Thus its coefficient is $T_{\sigma[0,1]}T_\beta a$, precisely the exceptional face coefficient in [F5]. Each other face retains the first vertex and coefficient; the alternating signs are the ordinary simplex signs. So $\Phi$ commutes with every boundary. Conversely, for an intrinsic generator $m\sigma$, lift $\sigma$ and choose $\widetilde\beta$ as above, and send it to $\widetilde\sigma\otimes T_\beta^{-1}m$. Replacing the lift by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$ replaces this coefficient by $g^{-1}T_\beta^{-1}m$, and the balanced relation gives the same tensor. Path independence follows as before. Each construction is additive on the direct sum, and their two composites are the identity on every simplex summand. They are therefore inverse chain isomorphisms. They also commute with based maps and coefficient morphisms: the image of $\widetilde\beta$ is a path to the first vertex of the image simplex, and the defining coefficient morphism commutes with its transport. This proves the actual target identification for the stated locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected $Y$, with no CW or local contractibility assumption on $Y$.

**Compute each word by the actual lifted path.** The lifted edge $e_j$ has endpoint $T_{x_j}e_0$, so its boundary is $e_0\cdot x_j^{-1}-e_0$. A positive occurrence after prefix $q$ traverses $T_qe_j=e_j\cdot q^{-1}$. A negative occurrence after prefix $q$ traverses the reverse of $T_{qx_j^{-1}}e_j$, giving exactly the negative contribution in the Statement. The endpoint differences telescope along these consecutive lifted edges, giving $\partial c_w=T_we_0-e_0=e_0\cdot w^{-1}-e_0$. In tensor coordinates its positive contribution is $e_j\otimes q^{-1}u$ and its negative contribution is $-e_j\otimes(qx_j^{-1})^{-1}u$. These are exactly the initial local coefficients on the successive oriented edges, because forward transport along a path of class $q$ is the action of $q^{-1}$ in [F5]. If $w u=u$, also $w^{-1}u=u$, and $\partial(c_w\otimes u)=0$. The boundary of each lifted relator disk is the same finite expression $c_{r_i}$, with its chosen orientation; its boundary is zero since $r_i=1$ in $\Gamma$. Thus the presentation complex really gives finite coefficient matrices, whose entries are the displayed finite word sums, including their inverse prefixes. No untyped identification of forward conjugation with a right module action is made.

**Build a comparison which is the actual map in degree one.** The based lift $\widetilde f:\widetilde P\to\widetilde Y$ exists by [F2]; uniqueness, or lifting a loop $g$, gives $\widetilde fT_g=T_{f_*(g)}\widetilde f$. Send the lifted presentation vertex to its actual singular image point, and each lifted generator edge to the singular path obtained by composing its parametrization with $\widetilde f$; extend right $R$-linearly to maps $b_0,b_1$. They commute with the degree-one boundary, because a path boundary is its final point minus its initial point. For each of the finitely many relator cells, $b_1\partial e_{r_i}$ is therefore a singular1cycle upstairs. The actual $H_1(\widetilde Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ in step2.1 supplies a finite singular2chain bounding it. Choose one for each relator and extend right-linearly to $b_2$. This is an actual augmentation-preserving comparison through degree2. Apply [F4] over $R^{\mathrm{op}}$: a right $R$-module $C$ becomes a left module by $r^{\mathrm{op}}c=cr$, while $A$ becomes a right module by $a\cdot r^{\mathrm{op}}=ra$. The flip $a\otimes c\mapsto c\otimes a$ identifies $A\otimes_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}C$ with $C\otimes_R A$, since $(ra)\otimes c=a\otimes cr$ becomes $c\otimes ra=cr\otimes a$. Step2.1 supplies all hypotheses of [F4], so $b\otimes1$ gives an isomorphism on first homology. Use step3.1 for the target singular tensor complex, and [F5] for cellular comparison on the CW domain $P$. Every presentation first-homology class is represented by a local edge cycle on $P^1$, and cellular comparison identifies that edge cycle with its actual singular cycle. The map $b_1$ sends it to its actual singular image under $f$, by construction. Hence this isomorphism is precisely $f_*$; the freely chosen $b_2$ changes no first-homology image. Neither a target CW structure nor a presentation spine is used.

**Identify the actual peripheral inclusion and its algebraic kernel.** Under cellular comparison [F5], the subdivided loop carrying initial coefficient $u$ is the sum of its successive oriented edge chains with transported coefficients, which is exactly step 3.2; subdividing or concatenating the finite edges does not change its homology class, by the prism relation in [F5]. Applying $f$ sends it to the loop class represented by $w$ in $Y$. Any other based loop representing that group element is based-homotopic to it; the homotopy transport at the fixed basepoint is the identity, so [F5] identifies their coefficient homology classes. Two choices of relator fillings give maps agreeing on generator edges and therefore give the same images of these cycles, independently of their behavior on $2$-cells. Apply this to the two loops of $j$. The isomorphism of step4.1 takes the two finite word cycles to $j_*[u\otimes\lambda]$ and $j_*[u\otimes\mu]$, in the stated order. In field coordinates they are the columns $U$; being cycles is $CU=0$, and $CB=0$ is the cellular boundary identity. Their kernel is precisely the preimage of $\operatorname{im}B$ under $U$. Finally appending two columns to $B$ adds exactly the dimension of their span modulo $\operatorname{im}B$, so their actual image has dimension one exactly when $\operatorname{rank}(B\mid U)=\operatorname{rank}B+1$. This uses the actual comparison, not the assumption that the presentation complex computes exterior $H_2$.

**Adjoint and knot applications, with the conventions retained.** For $A=\mathfrak{sl}_2(F)$ and its left coefficient action $gX=\rho(g)X\rho(g)^{-1}$, a generator action and its inverse have polynomial entries in the $SL_2$ entries: matrix inversion there is the polynomial adjugate. Every finite word sum in step 3.2 and each cycle column is consequently polynomial in those entries and in $u$. On the peripheral torus, forward transports are $\operatorname{Ad}\rho(\lambda)^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{Ad}\rho(\mu)^{-1}$ in [F5]. Apply [F6] to these two inverse matrices. Their meridian trace is still $t$, and their invariant vector is $\rho(\mu)^{-1}-tI/2=-u$ by the direct $SL_2$ identity $\rho(\mu)+\rho(\mu)^{-1}=tI$. Multiplying both peripheral basis vectors by $-1$ preserves their being a basis and does not change the common kernel line or its ordered coordinates. Thus the actual two torus classes with coefficient $u$ have exactly the asserted basis property, including characteristic different from2. An actual compact smooth knot exterior is a particular $Y$: its manifold charts give local path-connectedness and small simply connected coordinate neighborhoods, including half-space charts at its boundary, while its connectedness supplies path-connectedness. Its actual based torus inclusion is a particular $j$; the comparison applies with arbitrary finite presentation of its group. No CW structure on the exterior, deformation retract to a presentation complex, generic representation family, generic rank assertion or valuation/tree/surface conclusion has been presumed. All coefficient, lift and cellular choices are either supplied, finite, or covered by the declared full AC. This proves the stated actual degree-one and peripheral comparison.

citations.quote: Assume full AC. For any finite $r\ge0$, every polynomial in the entries of $r$ complex $2\times2$ matrices invariant under simultaneous conjugation by $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is a polynomial in traces of words in those matrices. For each given invariant only finitely many words are needed. If $Z\subseteq M_2(\mathbb C)^r$ is any closed reduced invariant algebraic subset, every invariant regular function on $Z$ is likewise a polynomial in the restricted word traces. In particular this applies to the representation variety of any finitely presented group in $SL_2(\mathbb C)$, with its determinant and relator equations. The assertion does not identify a nonsemisimple representation from its character or assert a generic representation over the character function field.

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ have a finite presentation. There is a finite list of words $w_1,\ldots,w_N\in G$ whose trace functions generate the coordinate ring of $X(E_K)$, so the map $[\rho]\mapsto(\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_1),\ldots,\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_N))$ is a closed embedding into $\mathbb C^N$, with defining ideal the kernel of the induced map $\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_N]\to\mathbb C[\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2)]^{SL_2}$. On the irreducible-character locus, equal trace coordinates determine conjugate representations; on the reducible locus, the quotient records the semisimplified diagonal character, not the possibly non-diagonalizable representative.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

Assume also Dependent Choice for the cited minimal-prime existence theorem. Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. Every affine algebraic set $X$ has a finite irredundant decomposition into nonempty irreducible closed subsets, unique up to permutation. These are its maximal irreducible closed subsets. The empty set has the empty decomposition.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $\rho:\Gamma\to SL_2(F)$ be a representation of a finitely generated group which is absolutely irreducible, meaning that no line is invariant under all its matrices after extension to any field containing $F$. Let $K\subseteq F$ be the subfield generated by the prime field and all traces $\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$, $g\in\Gamma$. There are words $A=\rho(a)$ and $B=\rho(b)$ and an element $\xi$ satisfying $\xi^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\xi+1=0$, with $\xi\ne\xi^{-1}$, such that over $F(\xi)$ the representation is conjugate by a matrix in $GL_2(F(\xi))$ to one whose generator matrices all lie in $SL_2(K(\xi))$. Thus the required model field has degree at most two over $K$. The entries are obtained by explicit finite formulas from $\xi$ and the traces of $A,B,AB,C,AC,BC,ABC$ for each generator matrix $C$. If $K(\xi)\ne K$, its nonidentity automorphism is realized on this model by simultaneous conjugation with one explicit matrix in $GL_2(K(\xi))$. In particular, suppose a projective point $z\in\mathbb P^r(K(\xi))$ is obtained from the model by a construction commuting with field automorphisms and invariant under simultaneous $GL_2$ conjugation. Then $z$ is defined over $K$. This last clause requires the stated compatibility and invariance; it asserts no analytic, homology-rank or quotient-existence theorem.

Let $G$ be any group and $\rho,\rho':G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ be representations with $$\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g)\qquad(g\in G).$$ If $\rho$ is irreducible, then $\rho'$ is irreducible and there is $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho'(g)=P\rho(g)P^{-1}$ for every $g$. If $\rho$ is reducible, it has the same trace character as its diagonal semisimplification $g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(\chi(g),\chi(g)^{-1})$, where $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^*$ is the character on a common invariant line. The two diagonal characters $\chi,\chi^{-1}$ determine the same semisimple conjugacy class. This is a pointwise statement; it does not assert that an irreducible character component admits a tautological representation over its function field or prove rational quotient descent.

derivations.claim: **A dominant source and an actual generic representation.** Let $R$ be the representation set and $\pi:R\to R/\!/SL_2$ its quotient. For this arbitrary finitely presented group, finite trace coordinates follow directly from [F1] and [F2]: express each of a finite list of invariant algebra generators as a polynomial in finitely many word traces and take the union of those finite word lists. They generate the same coordinate algebra and hence give its closed affine model. The closed set $\pi^{-1}(X)$ has finitely many irreducible components $Z_i$ by [F2]. The closures of their images cover $X$, because $\pi$ is onto. A nonempty irreducible set cannot be the union of finitely many proper closed subsets: split the union into its first member and the rest and repeat the defining irreducibility condition. Hence one $Z$ has dense image in $X$. Pullback injects $A$ into $\mathbb C[Z]$, since a function vanishing on that dense image vanishes on $X$. Put $F=\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[Z]$, so $K\subset F$. The coordinate generator matrices over $F$ satisfy determinant and relator identities by [F1]; thus they give an actual representation $\rho:G\to SL_2(F)$, whose word traces are the corresponding elements of $K$. No section of the quotient has been asserted.

**A trace certificate for absolute irreducibility.** Choose an irreducible complex character of $X$ and a representative using [F2]. The construction in [F3] supplies two words $a_0,b_0$ whose matrices have $a=\operatorname{tr}(a_0)$ different from $\pm2$ and whose normalized second matrix has both off-diagonal entries nonzero. Write $b=\operatorname{tr}(b_0)$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(a_0b_0)$ and $D=a^2-4$. In a basis diagonalizing the first word with eigenvalues $\xi,\xi^{-1}$, the product of the off-diagonal entries of the second is
$$q=\frac{abc-c^2-b^2-a^2+4}{a^2-4}.$$
Indeed its diagonal entries are $(c-\xi^{-1}b)/(\xi-\xi^{-1})$ and their complementary entry in trace $b$; their product minus one is the displayed expression by $\xi+\xi^{-1}=a$. Thus $D$ and the numerator of $q$ are nonzero regular functions on $X$. They remain nonzero in $F$. Over any field extension diagonalizing the first word, the nonzero product $q$ makes both off-diagonal entries of the second word nonzero. A common invariant line would have to be one of the two eigenspaces of the first, neither preserved by the second. This proves absolute irreducibility of the actual generic $\rho$, and also gives the same certificate at every complex character where these two regular functions do not vanish.

**Recover the model over at most a quadratic extension of $K$.** Adjoin one root $\xi$ of $T^2-aT+1$ to $F$ and put $L=K(\xi)\subset F(\xi)$. Apply the explicit normalization and recovery equations of [F3] to $\rho$ and these two words. Their coefficients are word traces in $K$, so they give generator matrices in $SL_2(L)$. These are the actual conjugated matrices over $F(\xi)$, since the four trace equations for each generator have nonzero determinant $q(\xi^{-1}-\xi)$. Their determinant, relator and word-trace identities therefore hold in $L$, which injects into $F(\xi)$. Denote this representation by $\sigma$. Absolute irreducibility follows from the same two-word certificate. If $L\ne K$, the explicit matrix $P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\q&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ conjugates every $\sigma(g)$ to $\tau\sigma(g)$: the recovery equations and the proof of [F3] apply unchanged with the larger coefficient field $K$. No assertion that $K$ equals its prime-field trace subfield is needed.

**Spread the actual matrices and specialize every point of an open set.** If $L=K$, express the finitely many generator entries and the required nonzero elements and their inverses as fractions in $A$ and invert the product of their nonzero denominators. Also invert $D$ and the numerator of $q$. This gives $B=A_f$. If $[L:K]=2$, each entry has a unique form $u+v\xi$ with $u,v\in K$. Clearing their finitely many coefficient denominators gives $B=A_f[\xi]\subset L$. The monic equation reduces every polynomial to degree at most one, and independence of $1,\xi$ over $K$ proves that this ring is exactly the displayed free rank-two quotient. For any additional nonzero $z\in L$, first clear its coefficient denominators. Its norm $z\tau(z)\in K^*$ is nonzero; after clearing and inverting its numerator, $z^{-1}=\tau(z)/(z\tau(z))$ belongs to $B$. Thus any finite further localization of $B$ can be achieved by enlarging $f$ in $A$. All matrix identities remain identities in $B$ because it is a subring of $L$. At a point $\chi\in D_X(f)$, in the quadratic case choose either complex root of $T^2-a(\chi)T+1$; evaluation gives a homomorphism $B\to\mathbb C$. In the degree-one case evaluate directly. The specialized determinant and relator identities give an actual representation. Its finite trace-coordinate list equals $\chi$, since those identities already hold in $B$; [F1] then gives equality of every word trace. The nonzero $D,q$ certificate proves irreducibility. The same argument works for every root and every point in this principal open, rather than merely for a constructible dense set.

**Projective descent with no quotient shortcut.** In the quadratic case the assumed compatibility and step 2.1 give $\tau z=z$ for the constructed projective point. Normalize one nonzero homogeneous coordinate to one. Each other coordinate is fixed by $\tau$; writing it as $u+v\xi$, with $u,v\in K$, gives $v(\xi-\xi^{-1})=0$, and hence $v=0$. The normalized coordinates lie in $K$. In the degree-one case this is automatic. They define a rational map on $X$ by clearing their finitely many denominators; one normalized coordinate is one, so they have no simultaneous zero there. Step 3.1 permits simultaneous clearing of any prescribed additional matrix or kernel-chart denominators, so later actual specializations may be checked on one smaller dense principal open. This proves all family and descent assertions, with no claim that a merely pointwise invariant assignment was rational before a construction was given.
